language.name: MongoDB
language.description: The document database of the MERN stack. Covers documents and CRUD, query and update operators, schema design, indexes and performance, the aggregation pipeline, transactions, replication and sharding, and Mongoose.

questions.question: What is MongoDB, and how is it different from a relational database like MySQL?
questions.answer:
Short answer: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database. It stores data as JSON-like documents in collections, instead of rows in tables with a fixed set of columns.

How it works: Main differences from MySQL:
Data shape: a document can hold nested objects and arrays, a row holds flat columns
Schema: flexible by default, MySQL needs ALTER TABLE for a new column
Relations: related data is often embedded in one document, MySQL uses JOINs across tables
Scaling: built-in replication and sharding for spreading data over many servers

Example: A blog post with its tags and author name fits in one document, so one read returns everything. In MySQL the same data needs posts, tags and post_tags tables and a JOIN.

Common mistake: Saying MongoDB has no schema or no transactions. Your app still has a schema (often enforced with Mongoose), and MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0.

Interview tip: Say you choose the database by data shape and access pattern, not by hype.

questions.question: What are a database, a collection and a document in MongoDB, and what are they called in SQL terms?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A database holds collections, a collection holds documents, and a document holds fields. In SQL terms they are a database, a table and a row.

How it works: The mapping:
Database: database (same idea)
Collection: table
Document: row
Field: column
Embedded document: a joined row from another table

Example: An app database "shop" can have a "users" collection and an "orders" collection. Each user is one document such as { name: "Ali", city: "Lahore" }.

Common mistake: Thinking you must create a collection before using it. MongoDB creates the database and the collection automatically on the first insert. That is handy, but a typo such as "uesrs" silently creates a new, wrong collection.

Interview tip: Add that unlike a table, a collection does not force every document to have the same fields, and that you can add rules with schema validation when you need them.

questions.question: What is BSON, and why does MongoDB store BSON instead of plain JSON?
questions.answer:
Short answer: BSON is Binary JSON. It is the format MongoDB uses to store documents and send them over the network. It is faster to scan and supports more data types than JSON.

How it works: What BSON adds over JSON:
More types: Date, ObjectId, Int32, Int64, Decimal128, binary data
Length prefixes: each document and string stores its size, so MongoDB can skip fields quickly
Typed numbers: JSON has only one number type, BSON knows integer from double

Example: When Node saves new Date(), the driver stores a real BSON Date, not a string. Date queries such as { createdAt: { $gte: start } } and date operators in aggregation then work correctly.

Common mistake: Storing dates as strings like "27/10/2026". They sort as text, not as dates, and date operators cannot use them.

Interview tip: Mention that BSON is not always smaller than JSON, because it stores field names and lengths in every document. That is why short field names can matter in very large collections.

questions.question: What is an ObjectId, and what information is hidden inside it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An ObjectId is the default 12-byte value MongoDB uses for _id. It is unique and roughly increases over time, so it can be generated by the driver without asking the server.

How it works: The 12 bytes are:
4 bytes: timestamp in seconds when it was created
5 bytes: a random value per process
3 bytes: a counter that increases for each new id

Example: You can read the creation time from the id itself, so many apps do not need a separate createdAt field just for sorting by insert order.

Common mistake: Treating ObjectIds as strictly ordered. Two ids created in the same second on different servers may not sort in creation order, and the timestamp has only second precision.

Interview tip: Say ObjectIds are not secret. They expose creation time and are partly guessable, so never use them alone as a password reset token or as protection for private links.

questions.question: What does a "flexible schema" mean in MongoDB, and what problems can it cause?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Documents in the same collection do not need the same fields or types. You can add a new field to new documents without migrating old ones.

How it works: MongoDB checks nothing about field names or types unless you add schema validation ($jsonSchema) or use a library like Mongoose. Each document carries its own field names.

Example: You add a "phone" field to the user sign-up form. New users have it, old users do not, and nothing breaks at the database level.

Common mistake: Letting the flexibility create messy data. One part of the code saves age as 25, another as "25". Queries like { age: { $gt: 18 } } then skip the string values and reports become wrong without any error.

Interview tip: Say "flexible schema does not mean no schema". Explain that you keep one schema in code (Mongoose) and, for important collections, also add database-level validation so other scripts cannot insert bad data.

questions.question: When would you choose MongoDB over a SQL database, and when would you pick SQL instead?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Pick MongoDB when your data is document-shaped, changes often and is read as whole objects. Pick SQL when you have many relationships, complex joins and strict constraints across tables.

How it works: Good fits:
MongoDB: product catalogs with different attributes, content and CMS data, user profiles, event logs, fast-changing startup apps
SQL: banking ledgers, accounting, inventory with many joins, heavy ad-hoc reporting

Example: An interview prep portal stores a language with its topics and questions. Each question is read on its own and the shape changes over time, so MongoDB fits well. A payroll system with employees, departments, salaries and tax rules joined in every report fits SQL better.

Common mistake: Answering "MongoDB is faster" or "SQL is old". Both are fast when modelled well. A bad schema is slow in either.

Interview tip: Mention that MongoDB now has transactions and SQL databases now have JSON columns, so the real question is which access patterns are most common.

questions.question: Some documents store price as the string "100" and others as the number 100. What goes wrong when you query and sort by price?
questions.answer:
Short answer: MongoDB compares values by BSON type first. A query for the number 100 does not match the string "100", and sorting puts all numbers before all strings.

How it works: Comparison order of types (lowest first):
Null and missing: first
Numbers: int, long, double and decimal compare by value
Strings: compared as text
Objects, arrays, ObjectId, Boolean, Date: later

Example: { price: { $gt: 50 } } returns only the numeric prices. Sorting by price gives 20, 100, 500, then "1000", "30" as strings in text order. A sales report silently misses every string price.

Common mistake: Fixing it in the frontend. The data stays wrong and every new query has the same bug.

Interview tip: Explain the fix in two steps: clean the data with an update pipeline that converts strings ($toDouble or $toDecimal), then prevent it with Mongoose types or $jsonSchema validation. You can find bad documents with { price: { $type: "string" } }.

questions.question: Your Node API compares two ObjectIds with === and it always returns false, even for the same user. Why, and how should you compare them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: ObjectIds are objects, and === on objects checks if they are the same object in memory, not the same value. Two separate ObjectId objects holding the same id are not ===.

How it works: post.author comes from the database as an ObjectId. req.user.id is often a string from the JWT. Even two ObjectIds with the same hex are different objects. Safe ways:
id.equals(otherId): works with an ObjectId or a 24-char hex string
String(a) === String(b): compares the hex text

Example: An "edit post" check if (post.author === req.user._id) always fails, so even the real owner gets 403. With a string id on one side, the check is also always false.

Common mistake: Using == and thinking it fixes it. It sometimes "works" because of type coercion to string, but it hides the real types and breaks again with two ObjectIds.

Interview tip: Mention that the same issue appears in arrays: likes.includes(userId) fails with ObjectIds. Use likes.some((id) => id.equals(userId)).

questions.question: Which number type should you use to store money in MongoDB, and why not a normal double?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use Decimal128, or store whole amounts in the smallest unit (paisa or cents) as integers. A normal double cannot store most decimal fractions exactly.

How it works: Numeric BSON types:
Int32: whole numbers up to about 2.1 billion
Int64 (long): very large whole numbers
Double: the default for JavaScript numbers, binary floating point
Decimal128: exact decimal values with 34 digits, made for money

Example: 0.1 + 0.2 in a double is 0.30000000000000004. Add 1,000 small payments and totals start to differ from the bank statement by a few paisa, which accountants will notice.

Common mistake: Using Decimal128 in the database but converting to a JavaScript number in the API and doing math there. The rounding error comes back in Node.

Interview tip: Say the integer approach (store 12550 for Rs 125.50) is simple and fast in Node. Mention that Mongoose has a Schema.Types.Decimal128 type, and that you must convert it with toString() before sending JSON.

questions.question: What is WiredTiger, and what does document-level concurrency mean for your application?
questions.answer:
Short answer: WiredTiger is MongoDB's default storage engine. It handles how data is written to disk, cached in memory and compressed. Document-level concurrency means two writes only block each other if they touch the same document.

How it works: The ones that matter:
Cache: keeps hot data and indexes in RAM (by default 50% of RAM minus 1 GB)
Compression: snappy for data and prefix compression for indexes saves disk space
Checkpoints and journal: data is flushed to disk regularly and the journal protects recent writes after a crash
MVCC: readers see a consistent snapshot and do not block writers

Example: Thousands of users update their own profiles at the same time. Each update locks only its own document, so they run in parallel.

Common mistake: Designing one "counter" or "settings" document that every request updates. All those writes now compete for the same document and become a bottleneck.

Interview tip: Mention that the working set (frequently used data plus indexes) should fit in RAM, otherwise reads go to disk and performance drops sharply.

questions.question: In MongoDB, which term is the equivalent of a row in a SQL table?
options: A collection
A document
A field
A cluster
questions.correctAnswer: A document
questions.answer:
Why B: Each record in MongoDB is a document, just like each record in a SQL table is a row.

Why not A: A collection is the equivalent of a table, the container of many documents.

Why not C: A field is one key-value pair inside a document, like a column value.

Why not D: A cluster is a group of servers (a replica set or sharded cluster), not a single record.

questions.question: You insert a document without an _id field from the Node.js driver. What happens?
options: The insert fails because _id is required
The document is saved with _id set to null
MongoDB gives it an auto-increment number like 1, 2, 3
A new unique ObjectId is added as _id automatically
questions.correctAnswer: A new unique ObjectId is added as _id automatically
questions.answer:
Why D: Every document needs a unique _id. If you do not give one, the driver (or the server) generates an ObjectId for you.

Why not A: _id is required, but it is filled in for you, so the insert succeeds.

Why not B: null is never used automatically. A second document with _id null would also break the unique _id index.

Why not C: MongoDB has no auto-increment. You would need your own counter collection for numbers like that.

questions.question: Your Node app saves { createdAt: new Date() }. Which BSON type is stored in MongoDB?
options: A string in ISO format, like "2026-10-27T10:00:00Z"
A Date, stored as milliseconds since 1970 (UTC)
A Timestamp, the same type the oplog uses
A number of seconds since 1970
questions.correctAnswer: A Date, stored as milliseconds since 1970 (UTC)
questions.answer:
Why B: The driver turns a JavaScript Date into a BSON Date, a 64-bit count of milliseconds since the Unix epoch in UTC.

Why not A: It only looks like an ISO string when printed. It is stored as a real date, so date queries work.

Why not C: BSON Timestamp is a special internal type used for replication, not for normal app dates.

Why not D: It is milliseconds, not seconds, and it keeps the Date type rather than a plain number.

questions.question: Which statement about a MongoDB collection is true by default?
options: Every document must have exactly the same fields
A collection must be created with a CREATE command before the first insert
Documents can have different fields unless you add schema validation
A collection can hold at most 16 MB of data
questions.correctAnswer: Documents can have different fields unless you add schema validation
questions.answer:
Why C: Collections have a flexible schema. Rules on fields and types only apply if you add validation (or use Mongoose in your app).

Why not A: That is how SQL tables work, not MongoDB collections.

Why not B: MongoDB creates the collection automatically on the first insert.

Why not D: 16 MB is the limit for one document, not for a whole collection.

questions.question: What can you learn from an ObjectId alone, without reading any other field of the document?
options: The user who created the document
The approximate creation time, to the second
The exact creation time, to the millisecond
The IP address of the server that created it
questions.correctAnswer: The approximate creation time, to the second
questions.answer:
Why B: The first 4 bytes of an ObjectId are a timestamp in seconds, and getTimestamp() reads it.

Why not A: An ObjectId knows nothing about users. You need your own field such as createdBy.

Why not C: The timestamp has only second precision. Ids made in the same second are ordered by the counter, not by time.

Why not D: Very old ObjectIds had a machine id part, but modern ones use a random value, and never an IP address.

questions.question: A collection has { v: "10" }, { v: 9 } and { v: null }. In what order does find().sort({ v: 1 }) return the v values?
questions.answer:
Why D: MongoDB sorts by BSON type first. Null comes before numbers, and numbers come before strings, so null, 9, "10".

Why not A: null is the lowest type, so it comes first in ascending order, not last.

Why not B: Strings never sort before numbers, even if the text looks like a smaller number.

Why not C: The number 9 sorts before every string, so "10" cannot come before 9.

Fix: Store numbers with one numeric type so sorting and range queries behave as expected.

questions.question: What are the basic CRUD methods in MongoDB, and what does each one return?
What does find() return in the Node.js MongoDB driver, and why do you call toArray() on it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: find() returns a cursor, a pointer to the results on the server. toArray() reads all batches from the cursor and gives you a normal JavaScript array.

How it works: The server sends results in batches (the first batch is up to 101 documents). The cursor fetches the next batch only when you need it. You can also chain sort(), skip(), limit() and project() before reading.

Example: For an API page of 20 questions you write find(filter).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).toArray(). For exporting 1 million rows to CSV you loop with for await (const doc of cursor) so memory stays small.

Common mistake: Calling toArray() on a huge result. All documents are loaded into Node memory at once and the process can run out of memory.

Interview tip: Mention that Mongoose hides the cursor: await Model.find() returns an array directly, and Model.find().cursor() gives you a stream for big exports.

questions.question: What is the difference between updateOne() and replaceOne()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: updateOne() changes only the fields named in update operators like $set and $inc. replaceOne() swaps the whole document for a new one, keeping only the _id.

How it works:
updateOne: needs operators ($set, $unset, $inc...), other fields stay as they are
replaceOne: takes a plain document, every field you leave out is removed

Example: A user changes only their city. updateOne({ _id }, { $set: { city: 'Karachi' } }) keeps name, email and password. If you used replaceOne({ _id }, { city: 'Karachi' }), the user would lose everything except _id and city.

Common mistake: Passing a plain object to updateOne. The Node.js driver throws "Update document requires atomic operators". Mongoose, however, wraps it in $set for you, so the same code behaves differently in the two libraries.

Interview tip: Say you use replaceOne only when you really have the full new document, for example saving a whole settings object from a form, and updateOne with $set for everything else.

questions.question: What is an upsert, and when would you use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An upsert is an update with { upsert: true }. If a document matches, it is updated. If nothing matches, a new document is inserted from the filter plus the update.

How it works: The new document gets the equality fields from the filter, the $set values, and the $setOnInsert values. The result has upsertedId so you know an insert happened.

Example: Daily stats: updateOne({ userId, day: '2026-10-27' }, { $inc: { questionsRead: 1 } }, { upsert: true }). The first read of the day creates the document with questionsRead 1, later reads increase it. No "check then insert" code is needed.

Common mistake: Running upserts without a unique index on the filter fields. Two requests at the same moment can both find nothing and both insert, giving duplicate documents.

Interview tip: Mention that you pair upserts with a unique index, and that a duplicate key error (code 11000) from a race can simply be retried, because the retry will then update the existing document.

questions.question: An updateMany() call returns matchedCount 50 but modifiedCount 30. What does that mean?
questions.answer:
Short answer: 50 documents matched the filter, but only 30 actually changed. The other 20 already had the values you tried to set, so MongoDB did not write them.

How it works:
matchedCount: documents that matched the filter
modifiedCount: documents whose content really changed
upsertedCount: 1 if an upsert inserted a new document

Example: You run updateMany({ plan: 'pro' }, { $set: { isActive: true } }). 20 pro users were already active, so they count as matched but not modified.

Common mistake: Using modifiedCount to decide if a record exists. If a user saves a form without changing anything, modifiedCount is 0 and the API wrongly returns "not found". Use matchedCount for "exists" checks and modifiedCount for "did anything change".

Interview tip: Mention that $inc and $push always change the document, so with those operators matched and modified are usually equal, while $set with the same value is a no-op.

questions.question: What is the difference between findOneAndUpdate() and updateOne(), and when do you need findOneAndUpdate()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Both update one document atomically. updateOne() returns only counts, while findOneAndUpdate() also returns the document itself, either before or after the change.

How it works: findOneAndUpdate options that matter:
returnDocument: 'before' (default) or 'after' in the Node driver
new: true does the same in Mongoose
projection: return only some fields
sort: which document to pick if many match

Example: A job queue. Each worker runs findOneAndUpdate({ status: 'pending' }, { $set: { status: 'running' } }, { sort: { createdAt: 1 }, returnDocument: 'after' }). Each worker gets a different job, because the find and the update happen as one atomic step.

Common mistake: Doing findOne() and then updateOne() as two calls for things like counters or job claiming. Another request can change the document between the two calls.

Interview tip: Use updateOne when you only need to know it worked (it is lighter), and findOneAndUpdate when the API must respond with the updated data.

questions.question: Two users click "Buy" at the same time for the last item. Your code reads the product, checks stock > 0, then updates stock. Stock becomes -1. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: This is a race condition. Both requests read stock 1 before either update runs, so both pass the check. Fix it by putting the check inside the update filter so the check and the change are one atomic operation.

How it works: A single updateOne is atomic for one document. With filter { _id, stock: { $gt: 0 } } and update { $inc: { stock: -1 } }, MongoDB checks and decrements in one step. The second request finds stock 0, matches nothing and gets matchedCount 0.

Example: Request A and B both read stock 1. A runs the atomic update and stock becomes 0. B's update matches no document, so you return "Sold out" for B.

Common mistake: Trying to fix it with a setTimeout, a flag in Node memory, or an extra findOne before the update. These fail with multiple requests or multiple servers.

Interview tip: Name the pattern "conditional update" and say read-then-write code is a red flag. For changes across several documents (stock plus order plus payment) mention a transaction.

questions.question: You call insertMany() with 1,000 documents and one of them has a duplicate key. What happens with ordered: true versus ordered: false?
questions.answer:
Short answer: With ordered: true (the default) MongoDB stops at the first error, so documents before it are saved and the rest are not. With ordered: false it skips the bad document and inserts all the others.

How it works: In both cases the call throws a MongoBulkWriteError. Nothing is rolled back.
ordered true: stops at the failing index
ordered false: tries every document, may run faster because the server can process them in parallel
err.writeErrors: lists the failed indexes and reasons
err.result.insertedCount: how many were saved (err.insertedCount in Mongoose)

Example: An admin bulk-uploads 160 questions and #40 duplicates an existing one. Ordered: only 39 saved. Unordered: 159 saved and you report "1 skipped".

Common mistake: Thinking insertMany is all-or-nothing. It is not a transaction, so a failed import can leave half the data in the collection.

Interview tip: Say you choose ordered: false for imports where documents are independent, and a transaction when the whole batch must succeed or fail together.

questions.question: What is bulkWrite(), and when is it better than running many separate update calls?
questions.answer:
Short answer: bulkWrite() sends a list of mixed operations (insertOne, updateOne, updateMany, deleteOne, replaceOne) to the server in one call. It saves network round trips when you have hundreds or thousands of writes.

How it works: The driver groups the operations into batches and sends them together. You get one result with insertedCount, matchedCount, modifiedCount, deletedCount and upsertedCount. Like insertMany, it supports ordered: false.

Example: A nightly job syncs 5,000 product prices from a supplier file. 5,000 separate updateOne calls at 20 ms each take 100 seconds. One bulkWrite with 5,000 updateOne operations finishes in a few seconds.

Common mistake: Putting await inside a loop for each write. Each call waits for a full network round trip, and on Atlas from a far region that can be 100 ms or more each.

Interview tip: Mention that bulkWrite is not atomic either: some operations may succeed before an error. If you need all-or-nothing, run the bulkWrite inside a transaction and keep the batch size reasonable.

questions.question: What is the difference between deleteMany({}) and drop() on a collection, and which would you use to clear test data?
questions.answer:
Short answer: deleteMany({}) removes every document one by one but keeps the collection, its indexes and its validation rules. drop() removes the whole collection at once, including indexes.

How it works:
deleteMany({}): slow on big collections, writes one oplog entry per document, indexes stay
drop(): almost instant, frees disk space, indexes and validators are gone
After drop(): the next insert creates the collection again, but without your indexes

Example: Clearing a 10 million document logs collection with deleteMany can take a long time and put load on the replica set. drop() takes a moment. But dropping a users collection removes the unique index on email, and duplicate users can appear until the index is created again.

Common mistake: Using drop() in test setup and then wondering why "duplicate email" tests pass. The unique index no longer exists.

Interview tip: For tests, say you use deleteMany({}) between tests (indexes stay) and drop or a fresh database between test runs. Also mention that Mongoose rebuilds indexes with Model.syncIndexes().

questions.question: Which method saves several new documents to a collection in one call?
options: insertOne()
insertAll()
insertMany()
saveMany()
questions.correctAnswer: insertMany()
questions.answer:
Why C: insertMany() takes an array of documents and inserts them in one request.

Why not A: insertOne() inserts a single document.

Why not B: There is no insertAll() method in MongoDB.

Why not D: There is no saveMany() method. In Mongoose, save() works on one document.

questions.question: Using the Node.js MongoDB driver, what does updateOne({ name: "Ali" }, { age: 30 }) do?
options: Sets age to 30 and keeps the other fields
Replaces the whole document with { age: 30 }
Throws an error because the update has no $ operator
Inserts a new document { name: "Ali", age: 30 }
questions.correctAnswer: Throws an error because the update has no $ operator
questions.answer:
Why C: The driver requires update operators. A plain object throws "Update document requires atomic operators".

Why not A: That is what { $set: { age: 30 } } does. Mongoose adds $set for you, but the plain driver does not.

Why not B: Replacing the document is the job of replaceOne().

Why not D: Nothing is inserted unless you pass upsert: true, and even then the update needs operators.

questions.question: No user has email "sara@example.com". What does updateOne({ email: "sara@example.com" }, { $set: { name: "Sara" } }, { upsert: true }) do?
options: Inserts { email: "sara@example.com", name: "Sara" } with a new _id
Does nothing and returns matchedCount 0
Inserts { name: "Sara" } only, without the email
Throws an error because no document matched
questions.correctAnswer: Inserts { email: "sara@example.com", name: "Sara" } with a new _id
questions.answer:
Why A: With upsert, the new document is built from the equality fields of the filter plus the $set fields, and an _id is generated.

Why not B: That is the result without upsert: true.

Why not C: Equality fields from the filter are copied into the new document, so email is included.

Why not D: Matching nothing is normal for an upsert. That is exactly when it inserts.

questions.question: Five documents have status "inactive". What does deleteOne({ status: "inactive" }) do?
options: Deletes all five documents
Throws an error because more than one document matches
Deletes nothing until you add a sort
Deletes only one of the five documents
questions.correctAnswer: Deletes only one of the five documents
questions.answer:
Why D: deleteOne() removes the first document it finds that matches the filter, and stops there.

Why not A: Deleting every match is the job of deleteMany().

Why not B: Several matches are allowed. deleteOne simply takes one of them.

Why not C: No sort is needed. If you need a specific one, use findOneAndDelete() with a sort.

questions.question: You call insertMany() with 5 documents (default options) and the 3rd one has a duplicate _id. How many documents are saved?
options: 0, because the whole insert is rolled back
5, because duplicates are skipped silently
questions.answer:
Why B: insertMany is ordered by default. Documents 1 and 2 are saved, the 3rd fails, and MongoDB stops, so 4 and 5 are not tried.

Why not A: insertMany is not a transaction, so nothing is rolled back.

Why not C: 4 would be the result with ordered: false, which skips only the bad document.

Why not D: A duplicate key always raises an error (code 11000). It is never skipped silently.

questions.question: In Node.js driver v6, what does await coll.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: id }, { $inc: { views: 1 } }) return when you pass no options?
options: The document after the update, with views increased
An object with matchedCount and modifiedCount
The document as it was before the update
Nothing, because the result is only in the server log
questions.correctAnswer: The document as it was before the update
questions.answer:
Why C: The default is returnDocument: 'before', and in driver v6 the method returns the document directly. So you get the old views value.

Why not A: You get the updated document only with { returnDocument: 'after' } (or { new: true } in Mongoose).

Why not B: Counts are what updateOne() returns, not findOneAndUpdate().

Why not D: The document is returned to your code. It is null only when nothing matched.

Fix: Pass { returnDocument: 'after' } when the API must show the new value.

questions.question: How do you sort, skip and limit query results, and in what order does MongoDB apply them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use sort() to order results, skip() to jump over some, and limit() to cap how many come back. MongoDB always applies them as sort, then skip, then limit, whatever order you chain them in.

How it works:
sort: orders results, 1 is ascending and -1 is descending
skip: ignores the first N results
limit: returns at most N results

Example: Page 3 of a question list with 10 per page is find(filter).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).skip(20).limit(10).

Common mistake: Paginating without sort(). Without a sort the order is not guaranteed, so the same question can show up on page 1 and page 2, and another one can be missed.

Interview tip: Add a unique field as a tie-breaker, for example sort({ createdAt: -1, _id: -1 }), so documents with the same createdAt always come in the same order.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.questions.find({ language: 'nodejs' })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1, _id: -1 })
  .skip(20)
  .limit(10)

questions.question: What are the comparison operators $eq, $ne, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in and $nin, and how do you use them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: They compare a field with a value inside a query filter. They are written as { field: { $operator: value } }.

How it works:
$eq / $ne: equal / not equal ({ field: value } is the short form of $eq)
$gt / $gte: greater than / greater than or equal
$lt / $lte: less than / less than or equal
$in / $nin: value is in / not in a list

Example: Find medium or hard questions created this year: { difficulty: { $in: ['medium', 'hard'] }, createdAt: { $gte: new Date('2026-01-01') } }. Two operators on one field make a range: { price: { $gte: 100, $lte: 500 } }.

Common mistake: Writing { price: { $gt: 100 }, price: { $lt: 500 } }. In a JavaScript object the second key overwrites the first, so only $lt is applied.

Interview tip: Mention that $ne and $nin also match documents where the field is missing, and that they usually cannot use an index well, so they are slow on big collections.

questions.question: How do $and and $or work, and when do you need to write $and explicitly?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Fields in one filter object are already joined with AND. $or matches if any condition is true. You need an explicit $and only when the same field or the same operator appears twice.

How it works:
Implicit AND: { status: 'active', role: 'admin' }
$or: { $or: [{ status: 'active' }, { role: 'admin' }] }
$in: shorter than $or when it is the same field with many values
Explicit $and: needed for two $or groups, because one object cannot have two $or keys

Example: A search where the user wants (title or tags contain "redis") and (difficulty easy or medium) needs $and with two $or arrays inside.

Common mistake: Writing { $or: [...], $or: [...] }. The second $or overwrites the first and half of the filter silently disappears.

Interview tip: Say that for $or, each branch should be able to use its own index, otherwise MongoDB falls back to a full collection scan.

questions.question: What is projection, and why can you not mix included and excluded fields in it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Projection chooses which fields come back from a query. You either list the fields you want (1) or the fields you do not want (0), but not both, because MongoDB would not know what to do with the fields you did not mention.

How it works:
Include mode: { name: 1, email: 1 } returns only those fields plus _id
Exclude mode: { password: 0 } returns everything except password
_id exception: you can exclude _id in include mode, { name: 1, _id: 0 }

Example: A public user list should never send passwords. find({}, { projection: { password: 0, resetToken: 0 } }) keeps the response small and safe.

Common mistake: Writing { name: 1, password: 0 }. MongoDB returns the error "Cannot do exclusion on field password in inclusion projection".

Interview tip: Mention that projection also helps speed: less data goes over the network, and if all requested fields are in an index the query can be "covered" and skip reading documents.

questions.question: How do you query a field inside a nested document, and how is { address: { city: "Lahore" } } different from { "address.city": "Lahore" }?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use dot notation, "address.city". Writing { address: { city: "Lahore" } } is an exact match on the whole embedded document, so it only matches if address has exactly that one field.

How it works:
Dot notation: matches if address.city is "Lahore", whatever other fields address has
Object match: the embedded document must be equal, same fields in the same order
Dot notation needs quotes: "address.city" is a string key in JavaScript

Example: A user has address { city: "Lahore", zip: "54000" }. { "address.city": "Lahore" } finds the user. { address: { city: "Lahore" } } does not, because zip is extra.

Common mistake: Building filters from a form object like { address: req.body.address } and getting no results when the user fills only some fields.

Interview tip: Mention that dot notation also works for array positions, such as "items.0.price", and that an index on "address.city" helps these queries.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.users.find({ 'address.city': 'Lahore' })          // matches
db.users.find({ address: { city: 'Lahore' } })      // only exact embedded doc

questions.question: How do queries on array fields work in MongoDB, for example matching one value, all values or an exact array?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A simple equality on an array field matches if any element equals the value. For other needs there are $all, $size and exact array matches.

How it works:
Single value: { tags: 'node' } matches if any element is "node"
$all: { tags: { $all: ['node', 'mongo'] } } needs both, in any order
Exact array: { tags: ['node', 'mongo'] } needs this array in this order
$size: { tags: { $size: 2 } } needs exactly two elements
Position: { 'tags.0': 'node' } checks the first element

Example: A question bank where each question has tags. A filter by one chip uses { tags: 'mongodb' }. A filter by several chips at once uses $all.

Common mistake: Using an exact array match when you meant $all. { tags: ['mongo', 'node'] } does not match ['node', 'mongo'] because the order differs.

Interview tip: Mention that $size only takes an exact number. For "more than 3 tags", store a tagsCount field or use { 'tags.3': { $exists: true } }.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.questions.find({ tags: 'mongodb' })
db.questions.find({ tags: { $all: ['mongodb', 'indexes'] } })
db.questions.find({ 'tags.3': { $exists: true } })   // 4 or more tags

questions.question: What is $elemMatch, and when do you need it instead of normal dot notation on an array?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $elemMatch makes all conditions apply to the same array element. Without it, each condition can be satisfied by a different element, which gives wrong matches.

How it works: For an array of objects like results: [{ subject, marks }]:
Dot notation: { 'results.subject': 'math', 'results.marks': { $gt: 80 } } means some element is math AND some element (maybe another) has marks over 80
$elemMatch: { results: { $elemMatch: { subject: 'math', marks: { $gt: 80 } } } } means one element is math with marks over 80

Example: A student has math 40 and english 90. The dot notation query wrongly returns them as "good at math". $elemMatch correctly leaves them out.

Common mistake: Not noticing the bug, because the wrong query still returns data that looks reasonable in small test sets.

Interview tip: Mention that $elemMatch is also a projection operator: it can return only the first matching element of an array instead of the whole array.

questions.question: What is the difference between { field: null }, { field: { $exists: false } } and { field: { $type: "null" } }?
questions.codeSnippet:
db.users.find({ phone: null })                  // null or missing
db.users.find({ phone: { $exists: false } })    // missing only
db.users.find({ phone: { $type: 'null' } })     // stored as null only

questions.question: Your search box sends user text straight into a query: { title: { $regex: req.query.q } }. What problems can this cause, and how do you fix them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is slow, it can break on special characters, and it can be abused. Escape the input, limit its length, and use a text or Atlas Search index for real search.

How it works: The problems:
Speed: a regex not anchored with ^ cannot use an index well, so every document is scanned
Wrong results: characters like . ( ) + ? have regex meaning, so "c++" can fail to parse
ReDoS: a crafted pattern can make the regex engine work for a long time
Case: regex is case sensitive unless you add the i option

Example: A user types "node.js (event loop)". The parentheses form a regex group and the dot matches any character, so results are strange or the query errors.

Common mistake: Thinking an index on title makes any regex fast. Only a case-sensitive prefix regex like /^node/ can use the index efficiently.

Interview tip: Show the escape function, and say for larger apps you would use a $text index or Atlas Search, which handle stemming and ranking.

questions.question: A login route runs User.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password }). An attacker sends { "password": { "$ne": null } }. What happens, and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: This is NoSQL injection. The JSON body turns the password into a query operator, so the filter becomes "password is not null" and the attacker logs in as that user without knowing the password.

How it works: express.json() turns the body into real objects, so req.body.password can be { $ne: null } instead of a string. MongoDB treats keys starting with $ as operators.

Example: Body { "email": "admin@site.com", "password": { "$ne": null } } matches the admin, because the admin's password is not null.

Common mistake: Thinking MongoDB is safe from injection because there is no SQL. Any place that puts user input directly in a filter is at risk.

Interview tip: Give layered fixes:
Cast input: String(req.body.email) or validate types with express-validator or Joi
Sanitize: Mongoose sanitizeFilter option or remove keys starting with $
Design: never query by password, find the user by email and compare with bcrypt.compare

questions.question: Which filter finds users whose age is 18 or more?
options: { age: { $gte: 18 } }
{ age: { $min: 18 } }
questions.correctAnswer: { age: { $gte: 18 } }
questions.answer:
Why B: $gte means greater than or equal, so 18 is included.

Why not A: $gt means strictly greater, so users who are exactly 18 are left out.

Why not C: $min is an update operator (and an aggregation accumulator), not a query operator.

Why not D: This matches only documents where age is the text ">= 18".

questions.question: A document has { tags: ["node", "mongo"] }. Which filter matches it?
options: { tags: ["mongo"] }
{ tags: "mongo" }
{ tags: ["mongo", "node"] }
{ "tags.1": "node" }
questions.correctAnswer: { tags: "mongo" }
questions.answer:
Why B: Equality on an array field matches if any element is equal, and "mongo" is one of the elements.

Why not A: An array value means an exact array match. ["mongo"] is not equal to ["node", "mongo"].

Why not C: Exact array matches care about order, and here the order is reversed.

Why not D: Index 1 is the second element, which is "mongo", not "node".

questions.question: What does db.users.find({}, { name: 1, email: 0 }) do?
options: Returns name and _id for every user
Returns every field except email
Returns only name, without _id
Throws an error about mixing inclusion and exclusion
questions.correctAnswer: Throws an error about mixing inclusion and exclusion
questions.answer:
Why D: A projection cannot include some fields and exclude others (only _id is an exception), so MongoDB rejects it.

Why not A: That would be the result of { name: 1 } alone.

Why not B: That would be the result of { email: 0 } alone.

Why not C: _id is returned by default unless you write _id: 0.

questions.question: Which filter finds users whose status is "active" OR whose role is "admin"?
options: { status: "active", role: "admin" }
{ $in: [{ status: "active" }, { role: "admin" }] }
{ $or: [{ status: "active" }, { role: "admin" }] }
{ status: { $or: ["active", "admin"] } }
questions.correctAnswer: { $or: [{ status: "active" }, { role: "admin" }] }
questions.answer:
Why C: $or takes an array of conditions and matches if at least one is true.

Why not A: Fields in one object are joined with AND, so both must be true.

Why not B: $in works on one field's values, it is not a top-level operator for whole conditions.

Why not D: $or cannot be used inside a field like that, and it also mixes two different fields.

questions.question: A student has scores: [{ subject: "math", marks: 40 }, { subject: "english", marks: 90 }]. Does { "scores.subject": "math", "scores.marks": { $gt: 80 } } match this student?
options: No, because math has only 40 marks
Yes, because each condition can match a different element
No, it throws an error without $elemMatch
Yes, but only if an index exists on scores
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, because each condition can match a different element
questions.answer:
Why B: Without $elemMatch, "subject is math" is matched by the first element and "marks over 80" by the second, so the document matches.

Why not A: That is the intended meaning, but you only get it with $elemMatch.

Why not C: The query is valid and runs. It just answers a different question.

Why not D: Indexes change speed, not which documents match.

Fix: { scores: { $elemMatch: { subject: "math", marks: { $gt: 80 } } } }

questions.question: A collection has { a: 1 }, { a: null } and { b: 2 }. How many documents does find({ a: null }) return?
questions.answer:
Why D: { a: null } matches documents where a is null and documents where a does not exist, so { a: null } and { b: 2 }.

Why not A: 1 would be right for { a: { $type: "null" } }, which needs the field to exist.

Why not B: null is a real value to match, so the query does not return nothing.

Why not C: { a: 1 } has a non-null value, so it is not matched.

questions.question: What do the $set and $unset update operators do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $set gives a field a new value and creates the field if it does not exist. $unset removes a field from the document completely.

How it works:
$set: { $set: { city: 'Lahore', 'address.zip': '54000' } } changes only these fields
$unset: { $unset: { tempToken: '' } } deletes the field, the value you give is ignored
Dot notation: works in both, so you can change one field inside an embedded document

Example: After a user verifies their email, you run updateOne({ _id }, { $set: { emailVerified: true }, $unset: { verifyToken: '' } }). The flag is set and the old token is removed in one atomic step.

Common mistake: Using $set with a whole embedded object, like { $set: { address: { city: 'Lahore' } } }. That replaces the full address object, so zip and street are lost. Use { $set: { 'address.city': 'Lahore' } } instead.

Interview tip: Mention that setting a field to null keeps the field with a null value, while $unset removes it. This matters for sparse and partial indexes and for $exists queries.

questions.question: What do the $inc, $mul, $min, $max and $currentDate operators do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: They change a field based on its current value, inside the database, in one atomic step. That avoids reading the value into Node and writing it back.

How it works:
$inc: adds a number (use a negative number to subtract)
$mul: multiplies the value
$min: sets the value only if the new value is smaller
$max: sets the value only if the new value is larger
$currentDate: sets the field to the server's current date

Example: When a user finishes a quiz, one update does it all: { $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $max: { bestScore: 85 }, $currentDate: { lastQuizAt: true } }. bestScore changes only if 85 beats the old best.

Common mistake: Reading bestScore in Node, comparing, then saving. Two quiz submissions at the same moment can overwrite each other, and the lower score can win.

Interview tip: Mention that $inc and $mul on a missing field create it ($inc starts from 0, $mul sets it to 0), so you do not need to set defaults first.

questions.question: What is the difference between $push and $addToSet?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $push always adds the value to the array, even if it is already there. $addToSet adds it only if an equal value is not already in the array.

How it works:
$push: allows duplicates, keeps the order you add in
$addToSet: no duplicates, like a set
$each: both need { $each: [...] } to add several values, otherwise the whole array is added as one element

Example: A bookmarks list uses $addToSet so pressing the bookmark button twice does not save the same question twice. A chat messages array or an activity history uses $push, because repeated items are valid.

Common mistake: Using $addToSet with objects that have changing fields. { questionId: 1, at: new Date() } is never equal to an existing entry because the time differs, so duplicates still appear.

Interview tip: Mention that for objects you check only the key in the filter instead: updateOne({ _id, 'bookmarks.questionId': { $ne: qid } }, { $push: { bookmarks: { questionId: qid, at: new Date() } } }).

questions.question: How do you remove items from an array with $pull, $pullAll and $pop?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $pull removes every element that matches a value or a condition. $pullAll removes all elements equal to any value in a list. $pop removes the first or last element.

How it works:
$pull: { $pull: { tags: 'old' } } or with a condition { $pull: { scores: { $lt: 50 } } }
$pullAll: { $pullAll: { tags: ['a', 'b'] } }
$pop: { $pop: { history: 1 } } removes the last, -1 removes the first

Example: When a user removes a bookmark: updateOne({ _id }, { $pull: { bookmarks: questionId } }). For an array of objects you can match by one field: { $pull: { cart: { productId } } } removes that product whatever its quantity.

Common mistake: Reading the array in Node, filtering it, and saving the whole array back. If the user adds a bookmark in another tab at the same time, that new bookmark is lost.

Interview tip: Mention that $pull removes all matching elements, not only the first. If an array has duplicates and you want to remove just one, $pull is not the right tool.
questions.codeSnippet:
await users.updateOne({ _id }, { $pull: { bookmarks: questionId } });
await carts.updateOne({ userId }, { $pull: { items: { productId } } });

questions.question: How do you keep only the latest 10 items in an array using $push with $each, $sort and $slice?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use $push with $each to add the item, and $slice to cut the array to a fixed size in the same update. $sort can order it first.

How it works: The modifiers run in this order:
$each: the values to add (required when using the others)
$position: where to insert (optional)
$sort: sorts the whole array after adding
$slice: keeps the first N (positive) or the last N (negative)

Example: Keep the last 10 quiz scores on the user profile: { $push: { recentScores: { $each: [{ score, at: new Date() }], $slice: -10 } } }. The array never grows past 10, so the document size stays small.

Common mistake: Pushing forever into an array like notifications or history. The document keeps growing, every read sends the big array, and it can reach the 16 MB limit.

Interview tip: Mention this is a simple "capped array" pattern. For full history, use a separate collection and keep only the latest few items embedded.

questions.question: What is $setOnInsert, and why is it useful with upsert?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $setOnInsert sets fields only when an upsert creates a new document. If the document already exists, those fields are left alone.

How it works: In one upsert you can mix operators:
$setOnInsert: values only for the first time, like createdAt or default plan
$set: values that should change every time, like lastSeenAt
$inc: counters that start from 0

Example: Tracking a user's daily login: updateOne({ userId, day }, { $setOnInsert: { firstLoginAt: new Date() }, $set: { lastLoginAt: new Date() }, $inc: { logins: 1 } }, { upsert: true }). firstLoginAt is written once and never overwritten.

Common mistake: Putting createdAt in $set. Every update then changes createdAt, so you lose the real creation time.

Interview tip: Mention that one field cannot be in both $set and $setOnInsert in the same update, because MongoDB reports a path conflict.

questions.question: What is the positional $ operator, and how do you update one matching element inside an array?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The positional $ stands for the first array element that matched the query filter. You use it in the update path, like "items.$.qty", to change only that element.

How it works: The array field must be part of the filter, so MongoDB knows which element matched. It updates only the first match, not all of them.

Example: A cart has items [{ productId: 'p1', qty: 1 }, { productId: 'p2', qty: 3 }]. To add one more of p2: updateOne({ _id: cartId, 'items.productId': 'p2' }, { $inc: { 'items.$.qty': 1 } }). Only p2 changes.

Common mistake: Using $ without putting the array in the filter. MongoDB then throws "The positional operator did not find the match needed from the query".

Interview tip: Mention the other two forms: $[] updates every element, and $[name] with arrayFilters updates every element that matches a condition. Also say that if the item is not in the cart, matchedCount is 0 and you then $push it.

questions.question: How do $[] and $[<identifier>] with arrayFilters work, and how are they different from the positional $?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $[] updates all elements of an array. $[name] updates every element that matches a condition you give in arrayFilters. The positional $ only updates the first element that matched the query.

How it works:
$: first element matched by the query filter
$[]: every element, no condition
$[x]: every element that passes the condition for x in arrayFilters
Nested arrays: you can use more than one identifier, like "orders.$[o].items.$[i].price"

Example: An order has 5 items and 3 of them are "pending". Ship all pending items in one call: updateOne({ _id }, { $set: { 'items.$[it].status': 'shipped' } }, { arrayFilters: [{ 'it.status': 'pending' }] }).

Common mistake: Using the positional $ for this and wondering why only one item changed.

Interview tip: Mention that the identifier must start with a lowercase letter and contain only letters and numbers, and that every identifier used in the update must have a filter in arrayFilters.

questions.question: A post has a likes array of user ids and a likesCount field. How do you make "like" safe so the same user cannot like twice and the count stays correct?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Put the "not liked yet" check in the filter and change both fields in one update. If the user already liked, nothing matches and nothing changes.

How it works: The filter { _id: postId, likes: { $ne: userId } } matches only if userId is not in the array. The update { $push: { likes: userId }, $inc: { likesCount: 1 } } runs atomically on that one document. Unlike works the same way with likes: userId in the filter, $pull and $inc -1.

Example: The user double-clicks the like button. Both requests reach the server. The first one matches and updates. The second one finds userId already in likes and gets matchedCount 0, so the count stays correct.

Common mistake: Using $addToSet for the array and $inc for the count without the filter. The array stays unique, but the count still goes up twice.

Interview tip: Mention that for very popular posts (100,000+ likes) the array gets huge, so you would move likes to a separate "likes" collection with a unique index on { postId, userId } and keep only likesCount on the post.

questions.question: What is an update with an aggregation pipeline, and when do you need it instead of normal update operators?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Since MongoDB 4.2, updateOne and updateMany can take an array of pipeline stages instead of an update document. You need it when the new value depends on other fields of the same document.

How it works: Allowed stages:
$set / $addFields: compute new fields with expressions
$unset / $project: remove or reshape fields
$replaceWith / $replaceRoot: replace the whole document
Field references: "$firstName" reads the current value of a field

Example: Build fullName from two fields for all users: updateMany({}, [{ $set: { fullName: { $concat: ['$firstName', ' ', '$lastName'] } } }]). A normal $set cannot do that, because it only takes fixed values.

Common mistake: Writing { $set: { fullName: '$firstName' } } without the array brackets. MongoDB then stores the text "$firstName" as the value instead of reading the field.

Interview tip: Mention that pipeline updates are great for data migrations, like converting price strings to numbers with $toDecimal, without pulling millions of documents into Node.

questions.question: Which update operator adds 1 to a views counter?
options: { $add: { views: 1 } }
{ $set: { views: +1 } }
{ $plus: { views: 1 } }
{ $inc: { views: 1 } }
questions.correctAnswer: { $inc: { views: 1 } }
questions.answer:
Why D: $inc adds the given number to the current value in one atomic step.

Why not A: $add is an aggregation expression, not an update operator, so this update fails.

Why not B: This sets views to exactly 1, it does not add to the old value.

Why not C: There is no $plus operator in MongoDB.

questions.question: A document has { tags: ["a", "b"] }. What is tags after updateOne({}, { $addToSet: { tags: { $each: ["b", "c"] } } })?
questions.answer:
Why C: $each adds each value separately, and $addToSet skips "b" because it is already there.

Why not A: Duplicates would only appear with $push.

Why not B: The nested array is what you get without $each, when the whole array is added as one element.

Why not D: $addToSet adds to the array, it does not replace it.

questions.question: A document has { items: [1, 2, 3, 2] }. What is items after updateOne({}, { $pull: { items: 2 } })?
questions.answer:
Why A: $pull removes every element equal to 2, so both 2s are gone.

Why not B: $pull does not stop after the first match.

Why not C: This would mean only the last 2 was removed, which is not how $pull works.

Why not D: This keeps the matches instead of removing them.

questions.question: What does updateOne({ _id: id }, { $unset: { age: "" } }) do?
options: Sets age to an empty string
Sets age to null
Removes the age field from the document
Throws an error because the value must be 1
questions.correctAnswer: Removes the age field from the document
questions.answer:
Why C: $unset deletes the field. The value you pass is ignored.

Why not A: The empty string is just a placeholder value, it is not written.

Why not B: To keep the field with null you would use { $set: { age: null } }.

Why not D: Any value is accepted. "", 1 and true all work the same.

questions.question: A document has { grades: [80, 85, 90] }. What is grades after updateOne({ grades: 85 }, { $set: { "grades.$": 100 } })?
questions.answer:
Why B: The positional $ points to the element matched by the filter, which is 85 at index 1, so only it becomes 100.

Why not A: $ is not the first element of the array, it is the first matched element.

Why not C: Changing every element needs $[], not $.

Why not D: $set replaces a value in place, it does not add a new element.

questions.question: A document has { n: 5 }. What happens when you run updateOne({}, { $set: { n: 10 }, $inc: { n: 1 } })?
options: n becomes 11
n becomes 10
n becomes 6
The update fails because two operators change the same field
questions.correctAnswer: The update fails because two operators change the same field
questions.answer:
Why D: MongoDB rejects updates where two operators target the same path, with the error "Updating the path 'n' would create a conflict at 'n'".

Why not A: MongoDB does not run $set and then $inc in order.

Why not B: Neither operator wins. The whole update is rejected.

Why not C: The $inc is not applied either, because the update never runs.

questions.question: What is the difference between embedding and referencing in MongoDB?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Embedding stores related data inside the same document. Referencing stores it in another collection and keeps only its _id, like a foreign key in SQL.

How it works:
Embedding: one read gets everything, and updates to the parent and its children are atomic
Referencing: data is stored once, but you need a second query, $lookup or populate() to read it

Example: A user's 2 or 3 addresses are embedded, because they are always shown with the profile. The user's orders are referenced, because there can be thousands and they are read on their own pages.

Common mistake: Copying a SQL design into MongoDB, with one collection per table and references everywhere. Every page then needs several queries, and you lose MongoDB's main advantage.

Interview tip: Say the rule in one line: "Data that is read together should be stored together." Then mention the limits: the 16 MB document size and how fast the embedded list grows.

questions.question: How do you decide whether to embed data or keep it in a separate collection?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Look at how the data is read and how big it can grow. Embed when it is small, bounded and usually read with the parent. Reference when it is large, unbounded, shared or often used on its own.

How it works: Questions to ask:
Read together: is it shown with the parent on most screens
Size: is the list bounded (a few) or can it grow without limit
Updates: does it change often and independently
Sharing: is the same data used by many parents (like a product in many orders)
Access: do you ever need to query it alone, across all parents

Example: Quiz attempt answers (10 to 20 items, read with the attempt) are embedded. Questions are referenced from attempts, because the same question is used by thousands of attempts and is edited by admins.

Common mistake: Deciding only by the "relationship type" from SQL classes. In MongoDB the access pattern matters more than one-to-many or many-to-many.

Interview tip: Mention that you list the main queries of the app first, then design the schema around them. This is the opposite order from SQL normalisation.

questions.question: How do you model one-to-few, one-to-many and one-to-squillions relationships in MongoDB?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Embed for one-to-few, store an array of ids in the parent for one-to-many, and store the parent id in each child for one-to-squillions.

How it works:
One-to-few: embed the children, for example a few phone numbers in a user
One-to-many: array of child ids in the parent, for example a course with 50 lesson ids
One-to-squillions: parentId in each child, for example millions of log lines with serverId

Example: A blog post has a handful of tags (embed), a list of around 30 related post ids (array of references), and possibly 100,000 comments (each comment stores postId).

Common mistake: Putting millions of child ids in a parent array. The parent becomes huge, slow to read and may hit 16 MB.

Interview tip: Mention that with "parent id in the child" you need an index on that field, like { postId: 1, createdAt: -1 }, so loading the comments of one post stays fast.

questions.question: How would you model a many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, in MongoDB?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Store an array of references on one or both sides, or use a separate "enrollments" collection when the link itself has data or there are very many links.

How it works: Options:
Array on one side: student.courseIds when a student has a few courses
Arrays on both sides: fast reads both ways, but two writes to keep in sync
Link collection: { studentId, courseId, enrolledAt, progress } like a SQL join table

Example: An LMS needs progress and enrolledAt for each student-course pair, and a popular course can have 50,000 students. A separate enrollments collection with indexes on { studentId: 1 } and { courseId: 1 } fits best.

Common mistake: Keeping arrays on both sides and updating them in two separate calls without a transaction. If the second call fails, the student shows the course but the course does not list the student.

Interview tip: Mention that if the link has its own data (date, status, progress), it should be a document of its own, not just an id in an array.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.enrollments.insertOne({ studentId, courseId, enrolledAt: new Date(), progress: 0 })
db.enrollments.createIndex({ studentId: 1, courseId: 1 }, { unique: true })
db.enrollments.createIndex({ courseId: 1 })

questions.question: Why should you add schema validation ($jsonSchema) to a collection when MongoDB has a flexible schema?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Validation stops bad data at the database level, no matter which app, script or person writes it. Mongoose rules only protect writes that go through your Mongoose models.

How it works: You attach a $jsonSchema to the collection with required fields, types, enums and ranges. Settings:
validationLevel strict: check all inserts and updates (default)
validationLevel moderate: skip checks on documents that were already invalid
validationAction error: reject bad writes (default)
validationAction warn: allow but log a warning

Example: A teammate runs a quick fix script in mongosh and saves difficulty "Hard" instead of "hard". Mongoose would not see it, but a $jsonSchema enum rejects it.

Common mistake: Turning on strict validation on an old collection with messy data. Updates to those old documents start failing. Start with warn, clean the data, then switch to error.

Interview tip: Mention that flexible schema is useful during early development, and validation is how you lock things down once the shape is stable.

questions.question: What is the 16 MB document limit, and which designs usually hit it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: One BSON document can be at most 16 MB. Designs that hit it usually have an array that keeps growing forever inside one document.

How it works: Typical causes:
Unbounded arrays: all comments, logs or messages inside one parent
Files in documents: images or PDFs saved as binary data
Activity history: every event pushed to the user document

Example: A chat app stores every message of a group inside the group document. A busy group with years of messages reaches the limit, and from then on every new message fails with "BSONObjectTooLarge".

Common mistake: Thinking "we will never reach 16 MB". Long before the limit, big documents are slow: every read sends the whole array over the network and uses a lot of cache.

Interview tip: Mention the fixes: move growing data to its own collection, keep a capped embedded array of recent items, use the bucket pattern, and store files in GridFS or object storage (S3) with only the URL in MongoDB.

questions.question: A blog stores all comments inside each post document. One post went viral, got 50,000 comments, and loading it is now very slow. How would you redesign it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Move comments to their own collection with postId, and keep only a small part in the post: the latest few comments and a comment count. This is the subset pattern.

How it works: The new design:
comments collection: { postId, userId, text, createdAt } with an index on { postId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
post document: recentComments (last 5) and commentsCount
Load more: the page fetches older comments in pages from the comments collection

Example: Opening the post now reads one small document and shows 5 comments instantly. "View all comments" loads 20 at a time with range pagination on createdAt.

Common mistake: Only adding $slice to the read query. The post document is still huge on disk and in cache, and it still grows toward 16 MB.

Interview tip: Mention the migration plan: copy comments to the new collection with a script, switch writes to both places, switch reads, then remove the old array. Also mention that adding a comment now updates two documents, so you either accept a short delay in recentComments or use a transaction.

questions.question: What is denormalization in MongoDB, and how do you keep duplicated data in sync?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Denormalization means copying a few fields from one document into another so a read needs only one query. The cost is that when the original changes, the copies must be updated too.

How it works: Ways to keep copies in sync:
Update both: change the original and then updateMany the copies, in a transaction if they must match exactly
Background job: a queue or change stream updates the copies a little later
Accept old values: some copies should never change, like the price in an old order

Example: Each question stores { topicName } as well as topicId, so the list page does not need a $lookup. When an admin renames a topic, you run updateMany({ topicId }, { $set: { topicName: newName } }).

Common mistake: Copying fields that change often, like a user's online status or follower count, into thousands of documents. Every change now needs a huge updateMany.

Interview tip: Say the rule: copy only fields that are read often and change rarely, like names and titles. This is called the extended reference pattern.

questions.question: What are common MongoDB schema design patterns, and what problem does each one solve?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Patterns are proven designs for common access problems. The most asked ones are subset, extended reference, computed, bucket, outlier and attribute.

The ones you need:
Subset: keep only the most used part embedded (latest 10 reviews), the rest in another collection
Extended reference: copy a few fields of a related document to avoid a lookup
Computed: store a precomputed value (likesCount, averageRating) instead of counting on every read
Bucket: group many small items into one document (one document per sensor per hour)
Outlier: handle a few huge cases differently (a celebrity with millions of followers)
Attribute: turn many optional fields into an array of { k, v } pairs so one index covers them

Example: A product catalog has many different specs per category. The attribute pattern stores specs: [{ k: 'ram', v: '16GB' }, { k: 'color', v: 'black' }] with one index on { 'specs.k': 1, 'specs.v': 1 }.

Common mistake: Naming patterns without the problem. Interviewers want "when and why".

Interview tip: Pick one pattern you really used and explain the before and after numbers.

questions.question: How would you design an orders collection so old orders stay correct when product prices or names change later?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Copy the product details that matter at purchase time (name, price, quantity) into the order line items. Keep productId only as a link for reporting.

How it works: An order is a historical record. The invoice must show what the customer actually paid, not today's price. Each item in the order stores:
productId: link back to the product
name: product name when bought
unitPrice: price when bought
qty: how many
Order totals: subtotal, discount, total, stored and never recomputed from current prices

Example: A course cost Rs 2,000 in January and Rs 3,000 now. The January order must still show Rs 2,000. If the order only stored productId, the old invoice would wrongly show Rs 3,000.

Common mistake: "Normalizing" orders by referencing products only. Reports, refunds and invoices change every time the catalog changes.

Interview tip: Say that this duplication is intentional: it is a snapshot, not stale data. The same idea applies to the shipping address, which should be copied into the order.
questions.codeSnippet:
{
  _id: ObjectId('...'),
  userId: ObjectId('...'),
  items: [{ productId: ObjectId('...'), name: 'Node.js Course', unitPrice: 2000, qty: 1 }],
  total: 2000,
  shippingAddress: { city: 'Lahore', line1: '...' },
  createdAt: ISODate('2026-01-15')
}

questions.question: What is the maximum size of a single BSON document in MongoDB?
options: 4 MB
64 MB
16 MB
There is no limit
questions.correctAnswer: 16 MB
questions.answer:
Why C: A single document can be at most 16 MB. Larger data needs another design or GridFS.

Why not A: 4 MB was the limit in very old versions of MongoDB, not today.

Why not B: 64 MB is not a document limit. It is closer to old chunk size defaults in sharding.

Why not D: There is a hard limit, and inserts or updates beyond it fail.

questions.question: A user has at most 3 delivery addresses, and they are always shown on the profile page. What is the best design?
options: Embed the addresses as an array in the user document
Store them in an addresses collection with userId
Store them in an addresses collection and keep their ids in the user
Save them as one JSON string field in the user
questions.correctAnswer: Embed the addresses as an array in the user document
questions.answer:
Why A: The list is small and bounded, and it is read with the user, so embedding gives one fast read and atomic updates.

Why not B: This works, but every profile view now needs a second query for only 3 small items.

Why not C: This adds both a second query and extra id syncing, with no benefit for 3 items.

Why not D: A string cannot be queried or indexed by city, and you must parse it in code.

questions.question: When saving an order, what should you do with the product price?
options: Store only productId and read the current price when showing the order
Keep a separate price-history collection and join it by date
Embed the whole product document, including its reviews
Copy the price and name into the order item at purchase time
questions.correctAnswer: Copy the price and name into the order item at purchase time
questions.answer:
Why D: The order is a snapshot. Copying the price and name keeps invoices correct even after the product changes.

Why not A: When the price changes, every old order would show the wrong amount.

Why not B: This can work but is complex and slow for something a simple copy solves.

Why not C: Reviews and other product data are not needed in an order and make it large.

questions.question: An app writes millions of log entries for each device. Where should the link between a log and its device be stored?
options: An array of all logs inside the device document
A deviceId field in each log document
One collection per device, named after the device id
An array of log ids inside the device document
questions.correctAnswer: A deviceId field in each log document
questions.answer:
Why B: This is one-to-squillions. Each log points to its device, and an index on deviceId keeps lookups fast.

Why not A: The device document would grow without limit and hit 16 MB.

Why not C: Thousands of collections waste resources and make queries across devices hard.

Why not D: Millions of ids in one array also grows without limit.

questions.question: A sensor sends one reading every second. Which pattern reduces the number of documents and the index size the most?
options: Outlier pattern
Polymorphic pattern
Extended reference pattern
Bucket pattern
questions.correctAnswer: Bucket pattern
questions.answer:
Why D: The bucket pattern groups readings, for example one document per sensor per hour with 3,600 readings, so there are far fewer documents and index entries.

Why not A: The outlier pattern handles a few unusually large cases, not regular high-volume data.

Why not B: The polymorphic pattern stores different shapes in one collection. It does not reduce document count.

Why not C: Extended reference copies fields to avoid lookups. It does not group many writes.

Fix: For pure time-series data, MongoDB time series collections apply bucketing for you.

questions.question: A collection uses validationLevel "moderate". What does that mean?
options: Only inserts are validated, updates are never checked
Inserts and updates are checked, except updates to documents that were already invalid
Invalid writes are saved but a warning is logged
All existing documents are checked once when the rule is added
questions.correctAnswer: Inserts and updates are checked, except updates to documents that were already invalid
questions.answer:
Why B: Moderate checks inserts and updates to valid documents, but lets you update old documents that already broke the rules.

Why not A: Updates to documents that already pass the rules are still validated.

Why not C: That describes validationAction "warn", which is a different setting.

Why not D: MongoDB never scans existing documents when you add a validator.

questions.question: What is an index in MongoDB, and why does it make queries faster?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An index is a sorted structure (a B-tree) that stores the values of one or more fields with a pointer to each document. MongoDB can jump to matching values instead of reading every document.

How it works: Without an index MongoDB does a collection scan (COLLSCAN) and checks every document. With an index it walks the B-tree (IXSCAN) to the matching keys, then fetches only those documents. Every collection has a unique index on _id by default.

Example: Finding one user by email in 1 million users. Without an index: 1 million documents checked, maybe a second or more. With { email: 1 }: a few index entries checked, a couple of milliseconds.

Common mistake: Indexing every field "to be safe". Each index uses RAM and disk, and every insert, update and delete must also update all indexes, so writes become slower.

Interview tip: Say you create indexes based on real queries, check them with explain(), and remove unused ones.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })
db.users.find({ email: 'ali@example.com' }).explain('executionStats')

questions.question: What is a compound index, and what is the prefix rule?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A compound index covers several fields in a fixed order, like { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 }. A query can use it if it filters on a prefix of those fields, starting from the first one.

How it works: For an index { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }:
Uses the index: a, then a with b, then a with b and c
Cannot use it well: b alone, c alone, b with c
Sorting: the index can return results already sorted in its order, or exactly the reverse

Example: { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } serves "latest quiz attempts of a user" both for the filter and the sort. It also serves "all attempts of a user", so a separate { userId: 1 } index is not needed.

Common mistake: Creating { createdAt: -1, userId: 1 } for the same query. The order of fields matters, and this one is much less useful for "one user's attempts".

Interview tip: Mention that a compound index makes single indexes on its prefix redundant, so you can drop them to save RAM.

questions.question: What is the ESR rule for ordering fields in a compound index?
questions.answer:
Short answer: ESR stands for Equality, Sort, Range. Put fields tested with equality first, then the fields you sort on, then fields with range conditions.

How it works:
Equality: exact matches like status: 'active' narrow the index to one section
Sort: in that section, keys are already in sort order, so no in-memory sort is needed
Range: $gt, $lt, $in on many values go last, so they do not break the sort order

Example: Query: find({ language: 'nodejs', difficulty: { $in: ['medium', 'hard'] } }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }). Best index: { language: 1, createdAt: -1, difficulty: 1 }.

Common mistake: Putting the range field before the sort field, like { language: 1, difficulty: 1, createdAt: -1 }. MongoDB then reads several index sections and must sort the results in memory, which shows as a SORT stage in explain().

Interview tip: Mention that $in with a few values sometimes acts like equality, so always confirm the best order with explain() on real data.
questions.codeSnippet: db.questions.createIndex({ language: 1, createdAt: -1, difficulty: 1 })

questions.question: What is a multikey index, and what limitation does it have?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A multikey index is an index on an array field. MongoDB creates one index entry for each element of the array, so a query on any element can use it.

How it works: MongoDB makes an index multikey automatically when it sees an array. Limits:
One array per document: in a compound index, at most one of the indexed fields can be an array in the same document
Size: a document with 500 tags creates 500 index entries
Covered queries: a multikey index usually cannot cover a query on the array field

Example: An index on { tags: 1 } lets find({ tags: 'mongodb' }) find questions quickly, whichever position the tag is in.

Common mistake: Creating { tags: 1, categories: 1 } when both fields are arrays. Inserting a document where both are arrays fails with "cannot index parallel arrays".

Interview tip: Mention that big arrays make multikey indexes heavy for writes, so for large lists a separate collection is often better.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.questions.createIndex({ tags: 1 })
