db.questions.find({ tags: 'mongodb' })   // uses the multikey index

questions.question: What happens when you create a unique index on a collection that already has duplicates, and how do documents without the field behave?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The index build fails with a duplicate key error until you remove the duplicates. Documents without the field are indexed as null, so only one such document is allowed.

How it works:
Existing duplicates: createIndex fails (E11000), nothing is created
New duplicates: insert or update fails with error code 11000
Missing field: counts as null, so the second document without the field also fails
Fix for optional fields: use a partial index, for example only where the field exists

Example: You add a unique index on username, but old users never set one. The second user without a username breaks the index. A partial index with { partialFilterExpression: { username: { $exists: true } } } solves it.

Common mistake: Relying only on code like "check if email exists, then insert". Two requests at the same time can both pass the check. Only a unique index really prevents duplicates.

Interview tip: Mention that you find duplicates first with an aggregation ($group by the field, then $match count > 1) before building the index.

questions.question: What is a TTL index, and how does it work?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A TTL (time to live) index deletes documents automatically after a set time. It is a single-field index on a Date field with the expireAfterSeconds option.

How it works: A background task runs about every 60 seconds and deletes documents whose date plus expireAfterSeconds is in the past. You can also set expireAfterSeconds: 0 and store the exact expiry time in the field itself.

Example: Password reset tokens should live for 1 hour: createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }). Sessions, OTP codes and temporary logs are other common uses.

Common mistake: Expecting deletion at the exact second. A document can stay for up to a minute or more after it expires, so your code must still check the expiry time when it reads a token.

Interview tip: Mention that TTL only works on a Date (or array of dates), documents without that field are never deleted, and TTL cannot be part of a compound index.

questions.question: What is the difference between a partial index and a sparse index, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A sparse index only includes documents that have the field. A partial index only includes documents that match any filter you choose. Partial indexes are newer and more flexible, so they are preferred.

How it works:
Sparse: skips documents where the field is missing
Partial: uses partialFilterExpression, like { status: 'active' } or { isDeleted: false }
Query rule: MongoDB uses a partial index only if the query filter is covered by the index filter

Example: 95% of orders are "completed" and you only search the "pending" ones. A partial index on { createdAt: 1 } with { status: 'pending' } is tiny and fast. Queries must include status: 'pending' to use it.

Common mistake: Querying without the condition, such as find().sort({ createdAt: 1 }), and wondering why the partial index is ignored. MongoDB cannot use it because the result could include documents the index left out.

Interview tip: Mention the classic use: a unique email index with { isDeleted: false } as the filter, so a soft-deleted user's email can sign up again. Note that a partial filter cannot use $exists: false.

questions.question: What are the costs of having too many indexes, and how do you find indexes that are not used?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Every index slows down writes, uses RAM and disk, and adds work for the query planner. Unused indexes give these costs with no benefit.

How it works: The costs:
Writes: each insert, update and delete must also update every index on changed fields
RAM: indexes should fit in memory with the working set, extra ones push data out
Planner: more candidate indexes to try when choosing a plan
Finding unused: db.collection.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]) shows how often each index was used since restart

Example: A questions collection has 12 indexes from old features. $indexStats shows 4 with zero use over a month. Dropping them makes bulk uploads clearly faster.

Common mistake: Dropping an index after checking a test server or right after a restart, when usage counters are still low. Check production over a full business cycle.

Interview tip: Mention you can hide an index first with db.collection.hideIndex(). The planner ignores it, and you can unhide it instantly if something becomes slow, instead of rebuilding it.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.questions.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])
db.questions.hideIndex('oldField_1')
// later, if nothing got slower
db.questions.dropIndex('oldField_1')

questions.question: How do a text index, a regex query and Atlas Search differ for building search in an app?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Regex is simple but slow and has no ranking. A $text index finds whole words with stemming and a relevance score. Atlas Search (Lucene based) adds fuzzy matching, autocomplete and better ranking.

How it works:
Regex: only a case-sensitive prefix like /^node/ uses an index well
Text index: one per collection, splits text into words, ignores stop words, sorts by textScore
Atlas Search: separate search index on Atlas, typo tolerance, autocomplete, highlights, via the $search stage

Example: A user types "evnt loop". Regex and $text both find nothing because of the typo. Atlas Search with fuzzy matching still returns "event loop" questions.

Common mistake: Expecting $text to match parts of words. Searching "mongo" does not find "mongodb", because $text matches whole words (with stemming), not substrings.

Interview tip: Say you would start with $text for a small app, and move to Atlas Search when users need autocomplete or typo tolerance, instead of building a separate Elasticsearch cluster.

questions.question: You have a unique index on email, but users still sign up as "Ali@Gmail.com" and "ali@gmail.com". How do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The unique index compares exact bytes, so different capital letters are different values. Either save emails in lowercase, or create the unique index with a case-insensitive collation.

How it works: Two fixes:
Lowercase on write: email.trim().toLowerCase() in code, or lowercase: true in the Mongoose schema
Collation index: { email: 1 } with collation { locale: 'en', strength: 2 }, which ignores case
Collation rule: queries must use the same collation to use that index

Example: With lowercase on write, both sign-ups become "ali@gmail.com" and the second one gets error 11000, so you return "Email already registered".

Common mistake: Fixing only new sign-ups. Old duplicates still exist, so first find and merge them, otherwise building the new index fails.

Interview tip: Say you prefer lowercasing in code because it is simple and every query works without collation, and you also lowercase the email at login so "Ali@Gmail.com" can still log in.

questions.question: Which index does MongoDB create automatically on every collection?
options: A unique index on _id
An index on createdAt
An index on every field
No index at all
questions.correctAnswer: A unique index on _id
questions.answer:
Why A: Every collection gets a unique index on _id, and it cannot be dropped.

Why not B: MongoDB does not add a createdAt field or index for you.

Why not C: Indexing every field would make writes very slow, so it never happens automatically.

Why not D: The _id index always exists.

questions.question: A collection has the index { status: 1, createdAt: -1 }. Which query can NOT use this index efficiently?
options: find({ status: "active" })
find({ status: "active" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 })
find({ createdAt: { $gt: someDate } })
find({ status: "active", createdAt: { $gt: someDate } })
questions.correctAnswer: find({ createdAt: { $gt: someDate } })
questions.answer:
Why C: createdAt alone is not a prefix of the index. The first field, status, is missing, so the index cannot narrow the search.

Why not A: status is the first field, a valid prefix.

Why not B: Equality on status plus a sort in the index order is the ideal use.

Why not D: Both fields are used, with equality first and the range second.

questions.question: You create a TTL index { createdAt: 1 } with expireAfterSeconds: 3600. When is a document deleted?
options: Exactly 3,600 seconds after createdAt
Some time after 3,600 seconds, usually within about a minute
At midnight every day
Only when you call a cleanup command
questions.correctAnswer: Some time after 3,600 seconds, usually within about a minute
questions.answer:
Why B: A background task checks for expired documents about every 60 seconds, so deletion happens shortly after expiry, not at the exact second.

Why not A: TTL is not precise to the second.

Why not C: There is no daily schedule. The task runs every minute or so.

Why not D: TTL deletion is automatic. No command is needed.

questions.question: A collection has a unique index on email. You insert two documents that have no email field. What happens?
options: Both are inserted, because missing fields are ignored by unique indexes
The second insert fails with a duplicate key error
MongoDB fills email with an empty string in both
Both are inserted, but the index is marked invalid
questions.correctAnswer: The second insert fails with a duplicate key error
questions.answer:
Why B: A missing field is indexed as null. The second document also has null, so the unique index rejects it.

Why not A: That is how a sparse or partial unique index behaves, not a normal one.

Why not C: MongoDB never adds fields to your documents.

Why not D: Indexes are not marked invalid. The write that breaks the rule fails.

questions.question: For find({ status: "active", age: { $gt: 25 } }).sort({ name: 1 }), which index is best by the ESR rule?
options: { age: 1, status: 1, name: 1 }
{ status: 1, age: 1, name: 1 }
{ name: 1, age: 1, status: 1 }
{ status: 1, name: 1, age: 1 }
questions.correctAnswer: { status: 1, name: 1, age: 1 }
questions.answer:
Why D: Equality (status), then Sort (name), then Range (age). Results come out already sorted by name.

Why not A: The range field first makes MongoDB scan a wide part of the index and sort in memory.

Why not B: The range on age comes before name, so the results are not in name order and need an in-memory sort.

Why not C: Starting with the sort field means the index cannot first narrow down to active users.

questions.question: A collection has the compound index { tags: 1, categories: 1 }. What happens when you insert a document where both tags and categories are arrays?
options: The insert fails with "cannot index parallel arrays"
It works normally and both arrays are indexed
Only the tags array is indexed
The arrays are converted to strings before indexing
questions.correctAnswer: The insert fails with "cannot index parallel arrays"
questions.answer:
Why A: A compound multikey index allows at most one array field per document, because the entries would multiply (every tag times every category).

Why not B: Two arrays in the same document are exactly what is not allowed.

Why not C: MongoDB does not choose one field silently. It rejects the write.

Why not D: MongoDB never converts arrays to strings for indexing.

Fix: Make one of the fields a single value, or use two separate indexes.

questions.question: What does explain() do in MongoDB, and what are its verbosity modes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: explain() shows how MongoDB runs a query: which index it picked, how many keys and documents it read, and how long it took. It is the first tool for checking a slow query.

How it works: The three modes:
queryPlanner: the chosen plan and rejected plans, without running the query
executionStats: runs the query and adds real counts and time
allPlansExecution: also shows stats for the plans that lost

Example: An API endpoint takes 2 seconds. You run the same filter with explain('executionStats') and see COLLSCAN with 500,000 documents examined, so you know an index is missing.

Common mistake: Testing explain() on a small local database with 50 documents. Everything looks fast there, and the problem only appears with production-size data.

Interview tip: Mention that in Mongoose you can call Model.find(filter).explain('executionStats'), and that Atlas shows the same information in its Query Profiler.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.questions.find({ language: 'nodejs' })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .explain('executionStats')

questions.question: In explain() output, what is the difference between COLLSCAN and IXSCAN, and which numbers should you look at?
questions.answer:
Short answer: COLLSCAN means every document was read. IXSCAN means an index was used. Then compare how many keys and documents were examined with how many were returned.

How it works: Key fields in executionStats:
nReturned: documents sent back
totalKeysExamined: index entries read
totalDocsExamined: documents read from storage
executionTimeMillis: time on the server
SORT stage: an in-memory sort, often a sign of a missing or wrong index

Example: nReturned 20, totalKeysExamined 20, totalDocsExamined 20 is ideal. nReturned 20 with totalDocsExamined 200,000 means MongoDB read 10,000 documents for each one it returned.

Common mistake: Seeing IXSCAN and assuming the query is good. An index on the wrong field can still examine thousands of keys to return a few documents.

Interview tip: Say the target is a ratio close to 1:1:1 between keys examined, documents examined and documents returned.

questions.question: What is a covered query, and why is it fast?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A covered query is answered completely from an index. The filter and every returned field are in the index, so MongoDB never reads the documents themselves.

How it works: Rules for a covered query:
Filter: all filter fields are in the index
Projection: only indexed fields are returned
_id: must be excluded with _id: 0 unless _id is in the index
In explain(): totalDocsExamined is 0 and there is no FETCH stage

Example: An "email exists?" check during sign-up: find({ email }, { projection: { email: 1, _id: 0 } }) with an index on { email: 1 } reads only the index.

Common mistake: Forgetting _id: 0. _id is returned by default and is not in the { email: 1 } index, so MongoDB has to fetch the document and the query is no longer covered.

Interview tip: Mention that covered queries cannot work with multikey indexes on the array field being returned, and that they matter most for hot, simple lookups.

questions.question: Why does skip() get slow for deep pages, and what is a better way to paginate?
questions.answer:
Short answer: skip(n) still walks over n entries before returning anything, so page 5,000 does a lot of work. Range (keyset) pagination continues from the last item seen and stays fast on every page.

How it works:
Skip pagination: sort, skip((page - 1) * size), limit(size), cost grows with the page number
Range pagination: remember the last createdAt and _id, then ask for items after them
Tie-breaker: sort by { createdAt: -1, _id: -1 } so equal dates have a fixed order

Example: An infinite scroll of questions sends the last item's createdAt and _id. The next query is { $or: [{ createdAt: { $lt: t } }, { createdAt: t, _id: { $lt: id } }] } with limit 20, which uses the index directly.

Common mistake: Showing "page 1 to 5,000" links on a huge collection. Users rarely need page 4,000, but bots crawling those links can load the database heavily.

Interview tip: Mention the trade-off: range pagination cannot jump to "page 37" directly, so it fits feeds and infinite scroll, while admin tables with small data can still use skip.

questions.question: What is an in-memory sort, and why is it a performance problem?
questions.answer:
Short answer: If no index provides the requested order, MongoDB loads the matching documents and sorts them in RAM. That shows as a SORT stage in explain() and gets slow and memory hungry as data grows.

How it works: A blocking sort must read all matches before returning the first one. Limits:
Memory: each blocking sort can use about 100 MB of RAM
Disk: since MongoDB 6.0, find and aggregate can spill to temporary files when it is over the limit, which is slower still
With limit(): MongoDB keeps only the top N in memory, which helps but still reads every match

Example: find({ language: 'nodejs' }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }) with only an index on { language: 1 } sorts every Node.js question in memory. An index on { language: 1, createdAt: -1 } returns them already in order.

Common mistake: Adding a separate { createdAt: -1 } index. MongoDB usually cannot combine one index for the filter and another for the sort.

Interview tip: Say you look for the SORT stage in explain() and fix it with a compound index that follows the ESR rule.

questions.question: How do you find slow queries in a production MongoDB?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use the database profiler or the slow query log, and on Atlas use the Query Profiler and Performance Advisor. Then run explain() on the queries they show.

How it works:
Slow query log: queries slower than slowms (100 ms by default) are written to the log
Profiler: db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 50 }) saves slow operations to system.profile
db.currentOp(): shows operations running right now, useful during an incident
Atlas Performance Advisor: suggests indexes based on real slow queries

Example: Users say the dashboard is slow. The profiler shows an aggregation on quizAttempts taking 3 seconds with a COLLSCAN. You add { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } and it drops to 20 ms.

Common mistake: Setting profiling level 2 (log everything) on a busy production server. It adds load and fills system.profile quickly.

Interview tip: Mention that you also log query time in the app (for example with Mongoose debug in development or APM tools in production), so you can link a slow endpoint to a slow query.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 50 })
db.system.profile.find().sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(5)

questions.question: The endpoint /orders?status=pending takes 3 seconds. explain() shows COLLSCAN, totalDocsExamined 2,000,000 and nReturned 20. What do you do, step by step?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read the exact query (filter, sort, limit), build an index that matches it, and confirm with explain() that it now uses IXSCAN with documents examined close to 20.

How it works: Steps:
Check the query: for example find({ status: 'pending' }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20)
Design the index: { status: 1, createdAt: -1 } by the ESR rule
Build it safely: on a big live collection, build in a quiet hour and watch load
Verify: explain() shows IXSCAN, no SORT stage, around 20 keys and 20 documents examined
Watch: check $indexStats and slow logs afterwards

Example: Before: 2,000,000 documents read, 3 s. After: 20 keys and 20 documents read, about 5 ms.

Common mistake: Adding only { status: 1 }. If 300,000 orders are pending, MongoDB still sorts them in memory, so the query stays slow.

Interview tip: Mention that you would also check whether the endpoint needs all fields, and add a projection so fewer bytes go over the network.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 })
db.orders.find({ status: 'pending' })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .limit(20)
  .explain('executionStats')

questions.question: How does the MongoDB query planner choose an index, and when would you use hint()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The planner runs the candidate plans for a short trial, picks the one that returns results with the least work, and caches that choice for queries with the same shape. hint() forces a specific index.

How it works:
Candidates: every index that could serve the filter or sort
Trial: plans race until one returns 101 results or finishes
Plan cache: the winner is reused for the same query shape
Re-planning: happens when the cached plan becomes much slower, or the cache is cleared (index changes, restart)

Example: A query on { status, createdAt } works well for months. Then the data changes and the planner starts choosing an index on { userId } for some shapes. Response times jump. explain('allPlansExecution') shows both plans and their work.

Common mistake: Adding hint() everywhere in app code. If data changes or the index is renamed, the hint keeps forcing a bad plan or causes an error.

Interview tip: Say you use hint() for debugging and comparing plans, and in code only as a last resort. The better fix is usually a more specific index or removing a confusing one.
questions.codeSnippet:
db.orders.find({ status: 'pending', userId })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .hint({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 })
  .explain('allPlansExecution')

questions.question: Why do queries using $ne, $nin, $where and unanchored $regex often perform badly?
questions.answer:
Short answer: These conditions cannot narrow the index to a small range. MongoDB ends up reading most of the index or the whole collection and checking each value.

How it works:
$ne / $nin: "everything except" matches almost all keys, so the index helps little
Unanchored regex: /mongo/ can be anywhere in the text, so every key must be checked
Case-insensitive regex: /^mongo/i cannot use the index range efficiently either
$where and $function: run JavaScript per document, very slow and not allowed on the Atlas free tier

Example: find({ status: { $ne: 'deleted' } }) on 1 million orders, where 990,000 are not deleted, reads almost every document even with an index on status.

Common mistake: Writing "not equal" filters out of habit. If only 3 statuses exist, { status: { $in: ['pending', 'paid'] } } can use the index as a few small ranges.

Interview tip: Mention the fix for soft deletes: store an isDeleted flag with a partial index, or move deleted documents to an archive collection, so normal queries stay simple equality.

questions.question: Your Node API loads 50 posts and then calls User.findById() for each author, so the page makes 51 queries. What is this problem called, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: This is the N+1 query problem. Fix it by loading all authors in one query with $in, or with Mongoose populate(), or with $lookup in an aggregation.

How it works: Each query has a network round trip, often 5 to 50 ms. 51 sequential queries can take a second or more, even when each one is fast.
$in: collect the author ids, run one find({ _id: { $in: ids } }), then map them back
populate: does the same $in query for you, so it is 2 queries in total
$lookup: joins in one aggregation on the server
Denormalize: store authorName in the post if it is needed on every list

Example: Using populate('author', 'name avatar') on the post list turns 51 queries into 2, and the page time drops from 900 ms to 60 ms.

Common mistake: Fixing it with Promise.all over the 50 findById calls. They run in parallel, but you still send 50 queries and use 50 connections from the pool.

Interview tip: Mention that you spot N+1 by turning on mongoose.set('debug', true) in development and counting queries per request.

questions.question: Which explain() stage means MongoDB read every document in the collection?
options: IXSCAN
FETCH
COLLSCAN
PROJECTION
questions.correctAnswer: COLLSCAN
questions.answer:
Why C: COLLSCAN is a collection scan: no usable index, so every document is checked.

Why not A: IXSCAN means an index was used to find the matches.

Why not B: FETCH reads the full documents after an index scan, only for the matching keys.

Why not D: PROJECTION only shapes the returned fields. It says nothing about how documents were found.

questions.question: executionStats shows nReturned: 10, totalKeysExamined: 10, totalDocsExamined: 0. What does this mean?
options: The query failed and returned cached results
An index was used and no documents were read, so it is a covered query
A full collection scan was done
The results came from the plan cache
questions.correctAnswer: An index was used and no documents were read, so it is a covered query
questions.answer:
Why B: Keys were read but zero documents were examined, so every returned field came from the index.

Why not A: A failed query shows an error, and MongoDB has no result cache for find.

Why not C: A collection scan would examine documents, so totalDocsExamined would not be 0.

Why not D: The plan cache stores which index to use, not the results themselves.

questions.question: With an index on { email: 1 }, which query is covered?
options: find({ email: "a@x.com" })
find({ email: "a@x.com" }, { email: 1 })
find({ email: "a@x.com" }, { email: 1, _id: 0 })
find({ email: "a@x.com" }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })
questions.correctAnswer: find({ email: "a@x.com" }, { email: 1, _id: 0 })
questions.answer:
Why C: The filter and the only returned field are in the index, and _id is excluded.

Why not A: With no projection, all fields are returned, so MongoDB must read the document.

Why not B: _id is returned by default and is not in this index, so a FETCH is needed.

Why not D: name is not in the index, so the document must be read.

questions.question: Why is find().sort({ createdAt: -1 }).skip(100000).limit(20) slow even with an index on createdAt?
options: skip() still walks over 100,000 index entries before returning the 20
limit() runs before skip(), so all documents are loaded
skip() can never use an index
MongoDB caches every page and the cache is full
questions.correctAnswer: skip() still walks over 100,000 index entries before returning the 20
questions.answer:
Why A: The index gives the order, but MongoDB still has to step over the first 100,000 entries one by one.

Why not B: The order is sort, then skip, then limit, whatever order you chain them.

Why not C: The index is used for the sort. The problem is the number of entries skipped, not the index.

Why not D: MongoDB does not cache result pages.

questions.question: For range pagination sorted by { createdAt: -1, _id: -1 }, which filter correctly gets the next page after the last item (lastAt, lastId)?
options: { createdAt: { $lt: lastAt } }
{ _id: { $gt: lastId } }
{ $or: [{ createdAt: { $lt: lastAt } }, { createdAt: lastAt, _id: { $lt: lastId } }] }
{ createdAt: { $lte: lastAt } }
questions.correctAnswer: { $or: [{ createdAt: { $lt: lastAt } }, { createdAt: lastAt, _id: { $lt: lastId } }] }
questions.answer:
Why C: It takes items with an older date, plus items with the same date but a smaller _id, exactly matching the sort order.

Why not A: Items that share the same createdAt as the last item but were not shown yet are skipped.

Why not B: This uses the wrong direction and ignores createdAt, so the order does not match the sort.

Why not D: This repeats the last item and every item with the same date on the next page.

questions.question: What does .hint({ status: 1 }) do on a find query?
options: It suggests the index, but the planner may still pick another one
It creates the index if it does not exist
It clears the plan cache for this collection
It forces the query to use that index, and errors if the index does not exist
questions.correctAnswer: It forces the query to use that index, and errors if the index does not exist
questions.answer:
Why D: hint() overrides the planner. If no index matches the hint, the query fails.

Why not A: It is not a suggestion. The planner does not choose against it.

Why not B: hint() never creates an index.

Why not C: Clearing the cache is done with planCacheClear, a different command.

questions.question: What is the aggregation pipeline, and how is it different from find()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The aggregation pipeline passes documents through a list of stages, where each stage changes the data and passes it on. find() can only filter, sort and choose fields, while a pipeline can also group, join, reshape and calculate.

How it works: Common stages:
$match: filter, like find
$group: group documents and calculate totals or averages
$project / $set: choose, rename or compute fields
$sort, $skip, $limit: order and page results
$lookup: join with another collection
$unwind: turn an array into one document per element

Example: "Average quiz score per language for this user" needs $match on the user, $group by language with $avg, and $sort. find() cannot calculate that, so you would otherwise load every attempt into Node.

Common mistake: Pulling thousands of documents into Node and calculating totals with JavaScript loops. The database can do it closer to the data and send back only the small result.

Interview tip: Compare it to a Unix pipe or an assembly line: each stage gets the output of the previous one.

questions.question: How does $group work, and what are the most used accumulators?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $group collects documents that share the same _id value into one output document, and accumulators calculate values over each group.

How it works: The _id says what to group by, for example '$language', or null for one group of everything.
$sum: total, or a count with { $sum: 1 }
$avg: average
$min / $max: smallest and largest value
$push: array of all values (duplicates kept)
$addToSet: array of unique values
$first / $last: value from the first or last document (sort before $group)

Example: Sales per city: { $group: { _id: '$city', revenue: { $sum: '$total' }, orders: { $sum: 1 }, customers: { $addToSet: '$userId' } } }.

Common mistake: Forgetting the $ before field names. { $sum: 'total' } adds the text "total", which counts as 0, so revenue shows 0.

Interview tip: Mention that the output field is always called _id, so you often add a $project stage to rename it, like { city: '$_id', _id: 0 }.

questions.question: Why should $match and $sort be placed as early as possible in a pipeline?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Only the first stages can use indexes, and every later stage works on fewer documents if you filter first. A $match at the start can use an index, a $match after $group cannot.

How it works:
Index use: $match and $sort at the start of the pipeline can use indexes, like a find
Less data: each later stage processes only the documents that survived the filter
Optimizer: MongoDB moves some stages forward for you, but not past stages that change the fields used

Example: A report for one month: putting { $match: { createdAt: { $gte: start, $lt: end } } } first reads 30,000 orders using an index. Putting it after $lookup and $unwind makes MongoDB join all 5 million orders first.

Common mistake: Filtering on a computed field in an early stage and expecting an index. A field created by $set or $group does not exist in any index.

Interview tip: Say you check pipelines with explain() too: db.orders.explain('executionStats').aggregate([...]) shows whether the first stage is IXSCAN.

questions.question: How does $lookup work, and how is it different from a SQL JOIN?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $lookup joins documents from another collection in the same database and puts the matches in a new array field. Unlike a SQL JOIN, the result is nested, not flat rows.

How it works:
from: the other collection
localField / foreignField: fields to match
as: name of the new array field
Pipeline form: let and pipeline allow extra conditions, sorting and limits on the joined data

Example: Orders with their customer: { $lookup: { from: 'users', localField: 'userId', foreignField: '_id', as: 'user' } }, then { $unwind: '$user' } to turn the one-item array into an object.

Common mistake: Not indexing foreignField. For each input document MongoDB searches the other collection, so a missing index there means a collection scan per document.

Interview tip: Mention that frequent $lookups may mean the schema should embed or copy some fields, and that $lookup into a sharded collection has limits in older versions.

questions.question: What does $unwind do, and what does the preserveNullAndEmptyArrays option change?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $unwind turns one document with an array into many documents, one per array element. By default, documents with an empty, null or missing array are removed from the results.

How it works:
Default: { $unwind: '$tags' } drops documents without tags
preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true keeps those documents (null stays null, an empty array field is removed)
includeArrayIndex: adds the position of each element as a field

Example: To count how many questions use each tag: $unwind '$tags', then $group by '$tags' with { $sum: 1 }. Each tag becomes its own row for grouping.

Common mistake: Using $unwind after $lookup and losing orders whose user was deleted. The lookup gives an empty array, $unwind removes the order, and the sales report total is wrong.

Interview tip: Mention that $unwind on big arrays multiplies the document count, so filter the array first ($filter or $match) and avoid unwinding just to count elements, because $size does that directly.

questions.question: What is the difference between $project and $addFields (or $set) in a pipeline?
questions.answer:
Short answer: $project defines the exact output shape: fields you do not mention are removed (unless you only exclude). $addFields and $set keep all existing fields and add or overwrite the ones you name.

How it works:
$project: include, exclude, rename and compute fields in one place
$addFields / $set: add computed fields, everything else stays
$unset: remove a few fields, the opposite of $set

Example: You want every order field plus a new "tax" field: { $set: { tax: { $multiply: ['$total', 0.17] } } }. With $project you would have to list every field you want to keep.

Common mistake: Using $project in the middle of a pipeline to add one field and then wondering why later stages cannot see fields like createdAt. $project removed them.

Interview tip: Mention that $project at the end is still useful to send only what the API needs, which shrinks the response.

questions.question: How can you return one page of results and the total count in a single aggregation query?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use $facet. It runs several sub-pipelines on the same input documents and returns all their results in one document, for example one for the page and one for the count.

How it works: A $match runs first, then $facet splits into:
data: $sort, $skip, $limit for the current page
total: $count for the number of matches
filters: optional $group stages for counts shown next to filter checkboxes

Example: A question list API returns { data: [20 questions], total: [{ count: 342 }] } in one round trip, so the frontend can show "Page 3 of 18".

Common mistake: Putting $facet first without a $match. Sub-pipelines inside $facet cannot use indexes, so every document goes into each facet, which is slow on large collections.

Interview tip: Mention that the whole $facet output is one document, so it must stay under 16 MB, and that for very large collections an estimated count or two separate queries can be faster.

questions.question: Write a pipeline that shows total revenue and order count per month for 2026, and explain each stage.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Filter to 2026 paid orders with $match, group by month with $group, then sort by month. Using real Date fields lets you group by date parts.

How it works:
$match: status paid and createdAt from 1 Jan 2026 to before 1 Jan 2027, can use an index on { status: 1, createdAt: 1 }
$group: _id is { $month: '$createdAt' }, with $sum of total and $sum: 1 for count
$sort: by _id so months come in order
$project: rename _id to month and round the revenue

Example: The result is 12 small documents like { month: 3, revenue: 482000, orders: 241 }, ready for a chart.

Common mistake: Ignoring the time zone. $month uses UTC by default, so an order at 2 AM on 1 March in Pakistan (UTC+5) is counted in February. Pass timezone: 'Asia/Karachi'.

Interview tip: Mention $dateTrunc (MongoDB 5.0+) as a clean way to group by day, week or month, and that months with zero orders are missing unless you add them in code or with $densify.

questions.question: What memory limits apply to aggregation pipelines, and how do $out and $merge help with heavy reports?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Blocking stages like $group and $sort can use about 100 MB of RAM each. Beyond that they need to spill to disk (allowDiskUse), which is slower. For heavy reports, save results with $out or $merge and read the saved collection.

How it works:
100 MB per stage: applies to $group, $sort, $bucket and similar stages
allowDiskUse: lets them use temporary files (on by default since MongoDB 6.0)
Output document: each result document must still be under 16 MB
$out: replaces a whole collection with the pipeline result
$merge: inserts or updates into an existing collection, good for incremental updates

Example: A nightly job runs a heavy pipeline over 50 million quiz attempts and $merges the results into a userStats collection. The dashboard then reads one small document per user in milliseconds.

Common mistake: Running the heavy report pipeline on every dashboard page load. It uses CPU and RAM for every visitor and slows the whole database.

Interview tip: Mention this is a "materialized view" pattern, and that $merge can update only changed users if you $match recent data first.

questions.question: How do you get the top 3 highest-scoring attempts for each user in one aggregation?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Group by user and use the $topN accumulator (MongoDB 5.2+) sorted by score. In older versions, $sort first, then $group with $push, then $slice the array to 3.

How it works:
$topN: { n: 3, sortBy: { score: -1 }, output: { score: '$score', at: '$createdAt' } }
Older way: $sort by score, $group with $push of each attempt, then $project with $slice of 3
Memory: $topN keeps only 3 per group, while $push keeps every attempt before slicing

Example: A leaderboard page shows each user's best 3 scores. With 10,000 users and 500,000 attempts, $topN returns 10,000 small documents without building huge arrays.

Common mistake: Using $push and $slice on large data. $push builds an array of every attempt per user first, which can hit the 100 MB stage limit or the 16 MB document limit for very active users.

Interview tip: Mention the related accumulators $top, $bottom, $firstN, $maxN, and that a $match on the time range before grouping keeps the work small.

questions.question: Find the employee with the second highest salary in MongoDB. How is it different from the SQL version?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Get the distinct salaries sorted from high to low, skip the first one, and take the next. Then find the employees with that salary. Working on distinct salaries matters, because two people can share the top salary.

How it works:
$group by salary: turns repeated salaries into one value each
$sort { _id: -1 } then $skip: 1 and $limit: 1: picks the second highest distinct salary
Second query (or $lookup): returns every employee with that salary
SQL version: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
Index { salary: -1 } keeps the sort fast on a big collection

Example: Salaries 90k, 90k, 70k, 50k. A plain sort + skip(1) returns the second 90k, which is wrong. Grouping first gives 90k, 70k, 50k, so the answer is 70k.

Common mistake: Using find().sort({ salary: -1 }).skip(1).limit(1) without handling duplicate salaries.

Interview tip: Ask whether "second highest" means the second distinct salary or the second row. Then mention $setWindowFields with $denseRank (MongoDB 5.0+) as a one-pipeline answer for N-th highest.

questions.question: Which aggregation stage filters documents, like the filter in find()?
options: $filter
$where
$find
$match
questions.correctAnswer: $match
questions.answer:
Why D: $match filters documents with the same query syntax as find().

Why not A: $filter is an expression that filters elements inside an array, not whole documents.

Why not B: $where runs JavaScript in queries and is not a pipeline stage.

Why not C: There is no $find stage.

questions.question: Three orders have city "Lahore", "Lahore" and "Karachi". What does [{ $group: { _id: "$city", total: { $sum: 1 } } }] return?
options: [{ total: 3 }]
[{ _id: "Lahore", total: 2 }, { _id: "Karachi", total: 1 }], in no fixed order
[{ city: "Lahore", total: 2 }, { city: "Karachi", total: 1 }]
An error, because _id must be an ObjectId
questions.correctAnswer: [{ _id: "Lahore", total: 2 }, { _id: "Karachi", total: 1 }], in no fixed order
questions.answer:
Why B: One output document per distinct city, with the group key in _id. $group does not sort its output.

Why not A: One total for everything needs _id: null.

Why not C: The key is always stored in _id. You need $project to rename it to city.

Why not D: In $group, _id can be any value or expression.

questions.question: A document is { name: "Ali", skills: ["js", "node"] }. What does { $unwind: "$skills" } output?
options: One document with skills still as an array
Two documents, each with skills as a full array
An error, because skills must be an object
Two documents, each with skills as one string
questions.correctAnswer: Two documents, each with skills as one string
questions.answer:
Why D: $unwind makes one document per element, so you get skills: "js" and skills: "node", each with name "Ali".

Why not A: That is the input. $unwind always splits the array.

Why not B: The array is replaced by a single element in each output document.

Why not C: $unwind expects an array, not an object.

questions.question: What type is the field created by $lookup (the "as" field)?
options: A single document, or null when nothing matches
A number with the count of matches
An array of matching documents, empty if nothing matches
An ObjectId of the first match
questions.correctAnswer: An array of matching documents, empty if nothing matches
questions.answer:
Why C: $lookup always writes an array, because many documents can match. No match gives [].

Why not A: You get a single object only after adding $unwind (or $first).

Why not B: A count needs an extra $size, or $count inside a pipeline lookup.

Why not D: $lookup returns whole documents, not ids.

questions.question: How does MongoDB run [{ $sort: { score: -1 } }, { $limit: 3 }]?
options: It sorts every document fully, then keeps 3
It combines them into a top-3 sort that keeps only 3 documents in memory
It runs $limit first, then sorts those 3 documents
It ignores $sort because $limit comes after it
questions.correctAnswer: It combines them into a top-3 sort that keeps only 3 documents in memory
questions.answer:
Why B: The optimizer merges $sort followed by $limit, so the sort only tracks the current top 3 instead of holding every document.

Why not A: That would waste memory, and the optimizer avoids it.

Why not C: That would return 3 random documents in sorted order, not the top 3.

Why not D: The order of stages is respected. $limit just limits the sorted result.

Fix: With an index on { score: -1 }, it can even read only 3 index entries.

questions.question: A document has { items: [] }. What happens to it in { $unwind: "$items" } with default options?
options: It is removed from the output
It is output once with items: null
It is output once with items: []
The pipeline fails with an error
questions.correctAnswer: It is removed from the output
questions.answer:
Why A: By default $unwind drops documents whose array is empty, null or missing.

Why not B: Even with preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true, the field is left missing rather than set to null.

Why not C: An empty array is never passed through by default.

Why not D: Empty arrays are valid input. They just produce no output documents.

Fix: Use { $unwind: { path: "$items", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } } to keep it.

questions.question: Is a single-document write atomic in MongoDB, and what does that mean in practice?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Yes. Any write to one document is atomic, even if it changes many fields and embedded arrays at once. Other readers see either the full old version or the full new version, never half.

How it works: One updateOne with $set, $inc and $push on the same document is applied as one unit. If the server crashes in the middle, the journal makes sure the change is either fully there or not there at all. updateMany is atomic per document, not for the whole set.

Example: Finishing a quiz updates score, completedAt and pushes the answers array in one updateOne. No one can ever see a completed attempt without its answers.

Common mistake: Thinking updateMany on 1,000 documents is all-or-nothing. If it fails after 600, those 600 stay changed.

Interview tip: Say this is why embedding is powerful: data that must change together can live in one document and needs no transaction.

questions.question: What are multi-document transactions in MongoDB, and when do you actually need them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Since MongoDB 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters), you can group writes to many documents and collections into one ACID transaction. You need them when several documents must change together or not at all.

How it works: Good reasons to use one:
Money: debit one account and credit another
Linked records: create an order, reduce stock and clear the cart
Uniqueness across collections: rules one index cannot enforce
Most other writes do not need them, because a single document is already atomic

Example: A wallet transfer of Rs 500 from Ali to Sara. Without a transaction, a crash after the debit loses Rs 500. With one, both updates commit together, or neither does.

Common mistake: Wrapping every request in a transaction "to be safe". Transactions hold locks, add latency and can fail with conflicts, so they make a busy app slower.

Interview tip: Say you first try to design the data so the change touches one document, and use a transaction only when that is not possible.

questions.question: How do you run a transaction with the Node.js MongoDB driver?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Start a session, call session.withTransaction() with an async function, and pass { session } to every operation inside it. withTransaction commits at the end, aborts on error and retries temporary failures.

How it works:
startSession: creates the session the transaction belongs to
withTransaction: runs your callback, commits, retries on TransientTransactionError and UnknownTransactionCommitResult
{ session }: every read and write must get it, or it runs outside the transaction
endSession: always call it in finally

Example: An order checkout inserts the order and decrements stock in one transaction. If stock is not enough, you throw an error and nothing is saved.

Common mistake: Doing non-database work inside the callback, like sending an email or charging a card. withTransaction may retry the callback, so the email could be sent twice. Do those after the commit.

Interview tip: Mention Mongoose has the same API with mongoose.startSession() and connection.transaction(), and keep the callback short and fast.

questions.question: Why do MongoDB transactions need a replica set, and how do you use them in local development?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Transactions are built on the oplog and on replica set features like snapshots and majority commits, so a standalone mongod does not support them. Locally, run a single-node replica set.

How it works:
Standalone: startTransaction fails with "Transaction numbers are only allowed on a replica set member or mongos"
Single-node replica set: start mongod with --replSet rs0, then run rs.initiate() once
Atlas: every cluster, even the free one, is a replica set, so transactions work there
Tests: mongodb-memory-server has MongoMemoryReplSet for this

Example: Checkout works on Atlas but crashes on a teammate's laptop with the error above. Converting their local mongod to a one-node replica set fixes it, with no code change.

Common mistake: Adding "if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') skip the transaction". Then the transaction code is never tested locally, and bugs only show up in production.

Interview tip: Mention that the connection string should include ?replicaSet=rs0 (or use directConnection for a single node) so the driver knows it is a replica set.
questions.codeSnippet:
# local single-node replica set
mongod --replSet rs0 --dbpath ./data
mongosh --eval "rs.initiate()"
# connection string
MONGO_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/interview-prep?replicaSet=rs0

questions.question: What is write concern, and what do w: 1, w: "majority" and j: true mean?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Write concern says how much confirmation you want before MongoDB reports a write as successful. Higher levels are safer but slower.

How it works:
w: 0: no acknowledgement at all (fire and forget)
w: 1: the primary applied the write
w: 'majority': most voting members have the write, so it survives a primary failure (default since MongoDB 5.0)
j: true: the write is in the on-disk journal before acknowledging
wtimeout: give up waiting after some milliseconds (the write may still happen)

Example: A payment record uses w: 'majority'. If the primary crashes right after a w: 1 write, that write can be rolled back when a new primary is elected, and the payment "disappears".

Common mistake: Using w: 0 for speed on important data. Errors such as duplicate keys are not even reported to your app.

Interview tip: Mention that a wtimeout error does not mean the write failed. It means the wait timed out, so the app must handle "unknown" results carefully.
questions.codeSnippet: await payments.insertOne(doc, { writeConcern: { w: 'majority', j: true } });

questions.question: What is read concern, and what is the difference between "local", "majority" and "snapshot"?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read concern controls how "safe" the data you read is: whether it could still be rolled back, and whether all reads in an operation see the same point in time.

How it works:
local: the newest data on the node, which might be rolled back later (default for normal reads)
majority: only data confirmed by most members, so it will not be rolled back
snapshot: inside a transaction, all reads see one consistent point in time
linearizable: reads reflect all writes acknowledged before the read, slowest option

Example: A report reads balances from three collections. With snapshot read concern in a transaction, all three reads match the same moment, so totals add up even while transfers are running.

Common mistake: Reading with "local" right after a failover and showing data that is later rolled back. For critical reads, pair w: 'majority' writes with majority reads.

Interview tip: Mention that read concern (how durable) is different from read preference (which member you read from). Interviewers often mix them on purpose.

questions.question: What is read preference, and what problems can reading from secondaries cause?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read preference decides which replica set member serves reads. Reading from secondaries spreads load, but secondaries can lag behind the primary, so you may read old data.

How it works: The modes:
primary: all reads from the primary (default)
primaryPreferred: primary, fall back to a secondary if it is down
secondary: only secondaries
secondaryPreferred: secondaries, fall back to the primary
nearest: the member with the lowest network latency

Example: A user updates their profile name, the page reloads and reads from a secondary that is 2 seconds behind. The old name appears and the user thinks the save failed.

Common mistake: Using secondary reads to "scale" a normal app. Each secondary still applies every write, and stale reads cause bugs that are hard to reproduce.

Interview tip: Say secondary reads fit analytics, reports and region-local reads where slightly old data is fine. For "read your own writes" use the primary, or causally consistent sessions, and maxStalenessSeconds to limit how old the data can be.

questions.question: What are the limits and costs of transactions in MongoDB, and how do you handle errors like TransientTransactionError?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Transactions should be short and small. They have a 60 second default time limit, can abort on write conflicts, and add latency. Temporary errors are labelled so you can retry the whole transaction.

How it works:
Time: transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds is 60 by default, longer ones are aborted
Write conflicts: if two transactions change the same document, one aborts
TransientTransactionError: retry the whole transaction from the start
UnknownTransactionCommitResult: retry only the commit
Size: very large transactions (thousands of documents) use a lot of cache and are slow

Example: During a flash sale, many checkouts update the same product stock document. Several transactions abort with write conflicts. withTransaction retries them, but latency rises.

Common mistake: Writing your own retry loop that retries on every error, including real errors like "out of stock" or validation failures. Retry only when the error has one of the labels above.

Interview tip: Mention that withTransaction already handles both labels, and that for hot documents you should reduce work inside the transaction or use a conditional single-document update instead.

questions.question: Checkout creates an order, reduces stock and clears the cart in three calls. The server crashed after the stock update, so stock went down but there is no order. How do you fix this?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Put the three writes in one transaction so they commit together or not at all. Also make the request safe to retry, so a client that resends after a timeout does not create two orders.

How it works:
Transaction: order insert, stock decrement and cart clear all use the same session
Conditional stock update: { stock: { $gte: qty } } inside the transaction
Idempotency key: the client sends a checkoutId, and orders has a unique index on it
After commit: send emails and push notifications only after the transaction succeeds

Example: Crash before commit: nothing is saved, stock is unchanged, the user retries. Crash after commit but before the response: the retry hits the unique checkoutId and the API returns the existing order instead of a second one.

Common mistake: "Fixing" it with a cleanup cron job that restores stock later. Stock is wrong in between, and the job can itself fail.

Interview tip: Mention the alternative when transactions are not available: a status field (pending, confirmed) with a background process that finishes or rolls back pending orders. This is called a saga or two-phase approach.

questions.question: What is optimistic concurrency control, and how do you use a version field to prevent lost updates?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each document has a version number. When you save, you include the version you read in the filter and increase it. If someone else saved in between, the version no longer matches and your update changes nothing.

How it works:
Read: get the document with version 7
Update: filter { _id, version: 7 }, update { $set: changes, $inc: { version: 1 } }
Check: matchedCount 0 means another write won, so reload and retry or tell the user

Example: Two admins edit the same question. Admin A saves first (version becomes 8). Admin B still has version 7, so B's save matches nothing and B sees "This question was changed by someone else, please reload" instead of silently overwriting A's work.

Common mistake: Relying on Mongoose __v for this. By default __v only protects array changes made through save(). You need the optimisticConcurrency: true schema option for full checks.

Interview tip: Compare it with pessimistic locking: optimistic is better when conflicts are rare, because nothing is locked while users are editing.

questions.question: What are ACID properties, and how does MongoDB provide them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: ACID means Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability: the guarantees that keep data correct when many operations run and something fails. MongoDB gives ACID for every single-document write, and since version 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters) also for multi-document transactions.

How it works:
Atomicity: all changes in a transaction happen, or none do
Consistency: rules like unique indexes and schema validation are never broken
Isolation: other operations do not see half-finished changes (snapshot isolation in transactions)
Durability: once acknowledged with writeConcern "majority", the data survives a crash
MongoDB: one document is always atomic, so embedding related data often removes the need for a transaction

Example: Moving 500 rupees from Ali to Sara means two updates. Inside a transaction, if the second update fails, the first is rolled back, so money is never lost.

Common mistake: Saying "MongoDB is not ACID". That was true for multi-document writes before 4.0, but not today.

Interview tip: Mention the cost: transactions are slower and need a replica set, so design the schema to keep related data in one document where it makes sense.

questions.question: Which of these is atomic without a transaction?
options: One updateOne that changes three fields of the same document
One updateMany that changes 50 documents
Inserting one document into each of two collections
One insertMany with 100 documents
questions.correctAnswer: One updateOne that changes three fields of the same document
questions.answer:
Why A: Every write to a single document is atomic, however many fields it changes.

Why not B: updateMany is atomic per document only. A failure halfway leaves some documents changed.

Why not C: Two collections means two separate writes, which need a transaction to be all-or-nothing.

Why not D: insertMany can save some documents and fail on others.

questions.question: What happens when you start a transaction on a standalone local mongod (not a replica set)?
options: It works normally
The writes run without atomicity and no error is shown
It fails, because transactions need a replica set or a sharded cluster
Only reads are allowed inside it
questions.correctAnswer: It fails, because transactions need a replica set or a sharded cluster
questions.answer:
Why C: Transactions depend on replica set features, so a standalone server rejects them with "Transaction numbers are only allowed on a replica set member or mongos".

Why not A: Standalone servers do not support transactions at all.

Why not B: MongoDB reports an error instead of silently dropping the guarantee.

Why not D: Read-only transactions fail too on a standalone server.

Fix: Run a single-node replica set locally with --replSet and rs.initiate().

questions.question: What does write concern { w: "majority" } mean?
options: The write must be applied to every member of the replica set
The write is acknowledged after most voting members have it
The write is saved to disk on the primary only
Most of the matched documents must be updated
questions.correctAnswer: The write is acknowledged after most voting members have it
questions.answer:
Why B: The primary waits until a majority of voting, data-bearing members confirm the write, so it survives a failover.

Why not A: Waiting for all members would fail whenever one member is down.

Why not C: That is closer to j: true with w: 1.

Why not D: Write concern is about servers confirming the write, not about how many documents changed.

questions.question: Using the Node.js driver inside withTransaction, you call orders.insertOne(doc) without passing { session }. What happens?
options: The driver adds the session automatically
The whole transaction fails to start
MongoDB throws an error at commit time
That insert runs outside the transaction and is not rolled back on abort
questions.correctAnswer: That insert runs outside the transaction and is not rolled back on abort
questions.answer:
Why D: Only operations given the session belong to the transaction. This insert is saved right away and stays even if the transaction aborts.

Why not A: The plain driver does not pass the session for you. Mongoose can do it only with the transactionAsyncLocalStorage option turned on.

Why not B: The transaction starts fine. The problem is that this one write is not part of it.

Why not C: No error is raised, which is why this bug is easy to miss.

questions.question: Two transactions update the same document at the same time. What happens?
options: One of them aborts with a write conflict, labelled TransientTransactionError, and can be retried
Both changes are applied and the last one wins
The second transaction waits until the first commits, then applies its change
MongoDB merges the two changes into one
questions.correctAnswer: One of them aborts with a write conflict, labelled TransientTransactionError, and can be retried
questions.answer:
Why A: MongoDB detects the write conflict and aborts one transaction. withTransaction retries it automatically.

Why not B: That would be a lost update, which transactions are designed to prevent.

Why not C: Plain writes outside transactions wait for locks, but inside a transaction a conflict aborts it instead of waiting.

Why not D: MongoDB never merges conflicting changes.

questions.question: Your app writes with w: 1 and reads with readPreference "secondary". A user saves their profile and the reload shows the old data. What is the most likely cause?
options: Secondaries only store indexes, not documents
The driver caches old query results
The secondary has not replicated the write yet (replication lag)
readPreference "secondary" ignores the query filter
questions.correctAnswer: The secondary has not replicated the write yet (replication lag)
questions.answer:
Why C: Secondaries apply writes from the oplog a little after the primary. A read right after the write can arrive before the change.

Why not A: Secondaries hold a full copy of the data.

Why not B: The MongoDB driver does not cache query results.

Why not D: Read preference only picks the server. The filter works the same everywhere.

Fix: Read from the primary for "read your own writes", or use causally consistent sessions.

questions.question: What is a replica set in MongoDB, and why would you use one?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A replica set is a group of mongod servers that keep copies of the same data. One is the primary and takes all writes, the others are secondaries that copy its changes. It gives high availability and protects against losing a server.

How it works:
Primary: receives every write and records it in the oplog
Secondaries: copy the oplog and apply the same changes
Failover: if the primary goes down, the others elect a new primary automatically
Typical size: 3 members, often in different zones or data centres

Example: On Atlas, every cluster is a 3-member replica set. When Atlas patches a server, it steps down the primary, a secondary takes over in a few seconds, and your app keeps working.

Common mistake: Calling a replica set a backup. If someone runs deleteMany({}) by mistake, the delete is copied to every member within seconds. You still need real backups.

Interview tip: Say replication is for availability and durability, and sharding is for scaling data size and write throughput. They solve different problems.

questions.question: How does automatic failover and primary election work in a replica set?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Members send heartbeats to each other every 2 seconds. If the primary does not answer for about 10 seconds, an eligible secondary calls an election, and the member that gets votes from a majority becomes the new primary.

How it works:
Heartbeats: every 2 seconds between all members
electionTimeoutMillis: 10 seconds by default before an election starts
Majority: a candidate needs votes from more than half of the voting members
Priority: members with higher priority are preferred, priority 0 can never become primary
Up to date: a secondary far behind in the oplog will not win

Example: In a 3-member set in two data centres, the primary's data centre loses power. The two remaining members still form a majority (2 of 3), so one of them becomes primary within about 10 to 12 seconds.

Common mistake: Running 2 members only. If one goes down, the other is only 1 of 2, not a majority, so it cannot become primary and writes stop.

Interview tip: Mention that during an election there is no primary for a few seconds, so apps should use retryable writes and handle short write errors gracefully.

questions.question: What is the oplog, and how do secondaries use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The oplog (operations log) is a special capped collection on each member that records every change to data. Secondaries read the primary's oplog and replay the same operations to stay in sync.

How it works:
Idempotent entries: an update with $inc is saved as the final value, so replaying it twice is safe
Capped size: old entries are removed when it is full
Oplog window: how many hours of changes it holds
Initial sync: a new member copies all data first, then catches up from the oplog

Example: A secondary is down for maintenance for 3 hours. If the oplog window is 24 hours, it catches up by replaying the missed changes. If it is down for 30 hours, the entries it needs are gone and it must do a full initial sync.

Common mistake: Running a huge updateMany on millions of documents during busy hours. Each changed document creates an oplog entry, which can shrink the oplog window and make secondaries lag.

Interview tip: Mention that change streams are built on the oplog, which is how apps can react to inserts and updates in real time.

questions.question: What is an arbiter in a replica set, and why is an odd number of voting members recommended?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An arbiter is a member that votes in elections but holds no data. An odd number of voters makes sure one side can always form a majority after a network split.

How it works:
3 voters: one can fail and 2 still form a majority
4 voters: still only one can fail (3 of 4 needed), so the 4th adds cost but no safety
Arbiter: a cheap tie-breaker, but it cannot store data or help with w: 'majority' writes

Example: A primary, a secondary and an arbiter (PSA). If the secondary goes down, the arbiter keeps the primary alive, but w: 'majority' writes cannot be confirmed by 2 data-bearing members, so they wait or time out.

Common mistake: Choosing PSA to save money for important data. With one data-bearing member down, you have no copy of the data and majority writes stall.

Interview tip: Say a 3-member replica set with data on all members (PSS) is the recommended setup, and arbiters are a last resort.

questions.question: What is the difference between replication and sharding?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Replication copies the same data to several servers for availability. Sharding splits the data across several servers so each holds only part of it, for scale.

How it works:
Replication: every member has all data, writes still go to one primary
Sharding: each shard has a slice of the data, writes are spread over many primaries
Combined: in production each shard is itself a replica set
Router: mongos sends each query to the right shards, config servers store where data lives

Example: An app with 200 GB and modest traffic needs only a replica set. An app with 20 TB of data and 100,000 writes per second needs sharding, because no single server can hold or write that much.

Common mistake: Sharding too early. It adds servers, a router and shard key decisions that are hard to change. Many apps are fine for years on one well-indexed replica set.

Interview tip: Say you would first scale vertically, add indexes and archive old data, and shard only when one replica set can no longer hold the data or the write load.

questions.question: What happens to your Node.js app during a failover, and what are retryable writes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: For a few seconds there is no primary, so writes fail with errors like "not primary" or network errors. Retryable writes let the driver resend such a failed write once to the new primary, without creating duplicates.

How it works:
Driver discovery: the driver monitors the replica set and finds the new primary
retryWrites=true: on by default in modern drivers and in Atlas connection strings
Safe retry: the server remembers the write's transaction number, so a retried insert is not applied twice
retryReads: reads are retried once too

Example: During an Atlas maintenance window, an order insert hits the old primary just as it steps down. The driver waits for the new primary and retries the insert, and the user sees no error.

Common mistake: Writing your own retry loop for inserts without an idempotency key. If the first insert actually succeeded but the reply was lost, your retry creates a duplicate order.

Interview tip: Mention that retryable writes retry only once, and updateMany and deleteMany with multi: true are not retryable, so your app should still handle errors.
questions.codeSnippet:
// Atlas connection strings already include it
mongodb+srv://user:CHANGE_ME@cluster0.example.mongodb.net/app?retryWrites=true&w=majority

questions.question: What is a shard key, and what makes a good one?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The shard key is the field (or fields) MongoDB uses to decide which shard stores each document. A good key spreads writes evenly and lets most queries go to only one shard.

How it works: What to look for:
High cardinality: many different values, so data can be split into many chunks
Low frequency: no single value used by a huge share of documents
Not monotonic: values should not always increase, or all inserts hit one shard
Query match: most frequent queries include the key, so mongos targets one shard

Example: For a multi-tenant app, { tenantId: 1, _id: 1 } spreads tenants over shards and every query for one tenant goes to one shard. A key on country would put most documents on the shard holding "PK" if most users are in Pakistan.

Common mistake: Picking a key only for even distribution, like a hashed _id, when every important query filters by userId. Then every query has to ask all shards.

Interview tip: Mention that since MongoDB 5.0 you can reshard a collection with reshardCollection, but it is a heavy operation, so the first choice still matters.
questions.codeSnippet: sh.shardCollection('app.orders', { tenantId: 1, _id: 1 })

questions.question: Why is a monotonically increasing shard key, like createdAt or ObjectId, a bad choice for an insert-heavy collection?
questions.answer:
Short answer: New values are always larger than old ones, so every new document goes to the chunk that holds the highest range, which lives on one shard. That shard takes all the inserts while the others sit idle.

How it works:
Ranged sharding: chunks hold continuous ranges, and the newest range is on one shard
Hot shard: one shard does all write work, so adding shards does not raise write throughput
Balancer: keeps moving chunks away, which adds even more load
Hashed sharding: hashing the key spreads new values randomly over all chunks

Example: A logging system shards on { createdAt: 1 }. At 50,000 inserts per second, one shard is at 100% CPU while the other 4 are almost idle.

Common mistake: Switching to a hashed key without thinking about queries. With { createdAt: 'hashed' }, a query for "last hour of logs" must go to every shard, because hashing destroys the order.

Interview tip: Mention the middle path: a compound key like { deviceId: 1, createdAt: 1 }, which spreads writes by device and keeps each device's data in time order.

questions.question: In a sharded cluster, what do mongos, config servers and shards do, and what is the difference between a targeted and a scatter-gather query?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Shards store the data, config servers store which chunk ranges live on which shard, and mongos is the router your app connects to. A targeted query goes to one shard, a scatter-gather query goes to all of them.

How it works:
Shards: each one is a replica set holding part of the data
Config servers: a replica set that stores the cluster metadata
mongos: reads the metadata, sends each query to the right shards and merges the results
Targeted: the filter includes the shard key, so only the shards owning those values are asked
Scatter-gather: no shard key in the filter, so every shard runs the query

Example: Orders sharded on { userId: 1 }. find({ userId }) goes to one shard. find({ status: 'pending' }) goes to all 10 shards, and the slowest one decides the response time.

Common mistake: Connecting the app directly to one shard. It would only see part of the data and skip the routing.

Interview tip: Mention that mongos is often run on the app servers themselves, and that scatter-gather is fine for rare admin reports but bad for hot user-facing queries.

questions.question: Your app has grown: one replica set holds 2 TB and writes are getting slow. Would you shard right away? What would you check first?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Not right away. First check if the slowness comes from missing indexes, bad queries or old data that could be archived. Shard when one replica set really cannot hold the data or the write load.

How it works: Checks before sharding:
Slow queries: profiler and Performance Advisor, fix COLLSCANs and in-memory sorts
Indexes: drop unused ones, they slow every write
Working set: if hot data plus indexes do not fit in RAM, add RAM or a bigger tier
Old data: move orders older than 2 years to an archive collection or Atlas Online Archive
Write pattern: one hot document or a huge updateMany can be the real problem

Example: The team finds 6 unused indexes and 1.2 TB of logs from 2021. Dropping the indexes and archiving the logs doubles write speed, and sharding is not needed for another year.

Common mistake: Sharding with a rushed shard key during an incident. A poor key causes hot shards and is costly to change later.

Interview tip: Say that if you do shard, you start with the collections that need it, pick the key from the main query patterns, and test with production-like data first.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of members recommended for a production replica set?
questions.answer:
Why C: Three members let one fail while the other two still form a majority and elect a primary.

Why not A: One member has no copy of the data and no failover. It is not a replica set in practice.

Why not B: With two members, if one fails the other is not a majority, so no primary can be elected.

Why not D: Five members are fine for extra safety, but they are not the minimum.

questions.question: In a replica set, which member accepts write operations?
options: Any member, whichever is closest
Only the primary
Only secondaries, to keep load off the primary
The arbiter
questions.correctAnswer: Only the primary
questions.answer:
Why B: All writes go to the primary, which records them in the oplog for the secondaries to copy.

Why not A: Picking the nearest member is a read preference option. Writes cannot go anywhere but the primary.

Why not C: Secondaries reject direct writes. They only apply changes copied from the primary.

Why not D: An arbiter holds no data at all. It only votes in elections.

questions.question: A 3-member replica set loses 2 members. What happens to the remaining member?
options: It becomes primary and keeps accepting writes
It deletes its data to avoid conflicts
It switches to standalone mode automatically
It stays a secondary, so writes fail but reads with a secondary read preference still work
questions.correctAnswer: It stays a secondary, so writes fail but reads with a secondary read preference still work
questions.answer:
Why D: One member out of three is not a majority, so it cannot become primary. It can still serve reads if the app allows secondary reads.

Why not A: Becoming primary needs votes from a majority of the set, and 1 of 3 is not a majority.

Why not B: Data is never deleted because of an outage.

Why not C: There is no automatic switch to standalone. An admin would have to reconfigure the set by force.

questions.question: What is the role of mongos in a sharded cluster?
options: It stores one part of the data
It routes queries from the app to the right shards and merges the results
It stores the metadata about which chunks live on which shard
It takes nightly backups of every shard
questions.correctAnswer: It routes queries from the app to the right shards and merges the results
questions.answer:
Why B: mongos is the query router. The app connects to it, and it decides which shards to ask.

Why not A: Shards store the data, not mongos.

Why not C: Config servers store the metadata. mongos only caches and reads it.

Why not D: Backups are done by tools like Atlas backups or mongodump, not mongos.

questions.question: An insert-heavy collection is sharded on a ranged key { createdAt: 1 }. What problem appears?
options: Queries by date can never be sent to a single shard
createdAt is not allowed as a shard key
All new inserts go to the chunk with the highest range, on one shard
The balancer deletes old documents to make space
questions.correctAnswer: All new inserts go to the chunk with the highest range, on one shard
questions.answer:
Why C: Each new createdAt is larger than the last, so inserts always land in the last chunk, creating a hot shard.

Why not A: Range queries on createdAt actually target only a few shards with this key. The problem is writes.

Why not B: A date field is allowed. It is just a poor choice for insert-heavy data.

Why not D: The balancer moves chunks between shards. It never deletes documents.

questions.question: A collection is sharded on { userId: "hashed" }. How does mongos run find({ email: "a@x.com" })?
options: It sends it to every shard and merges the results (scatter-gather)
It sends it to one shard, using a hash of the email
It fails, because the filter does not include the shard key
It reads the answer from the config servers
questions.correctAnswer: It sends it to every shard and merges the results (scatter-gather)
questions.answer:
Why A: The filter has no userId, so mongos cannot know which shard holds the document and must ask all of them.

Why not B: Only the shard key (userId) is hashed for routing. Hashing the email tells mongos nothing.

Why not C: Queries without the shard key are allowed. They are just slower.

Why not D: Config servers store chunk metadata, not your documents.

questions.question: What is Mongoose, and why would you use it instead of the plain MongoDB Node.js driver?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Mongoose is an ODM (Object Data Modeling) library for MongoDB in Node.js. It adds schemas, validation, type casting, middleware and helpers like populate() on top of the official driver.

How it works: What Mongoose gives you:
Schema: one place that defines fields, types and defaults
Validation: required, min, max, enum and custom rules before saving
Casting: turns "25" into 25 and id strings into ObjectIds
Middleware: hooks like pre('save') for hashing passwords
populate: loads referenced documents for you

Example: In a MERN app, a User model with email: { type: String, required: true, unique: true, lowercase: true } handles validation and formatting in one line instead of checks in every route.
