Common mistake: Thinking Mongoose validation protects the database. It only runs for writes made through Mongoose models, not for scripts or other apps using the driver.

Interview tip: Say the driver is lighter and faster for simple or very high-throughput work, while Mongoose gives structure for typical app code. Mongoose uses the driver underneath.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Schema, a Model and a Document in Mongoose?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A Schema describes the shape and rules. A Model is a class built from the schema and linked to a collection. A Document is one instance of the model, one record.

How it works:
Schema: new mongoose.Schema({...}), fields, types, validators, hooks, methods
Model: mongoose.model('User', userSchema), has static methods like find, create, updateOne
Document: new User({...}) or a result of findOne, has save(), validate(), toJSON()
Collection name: the model name is lowercased and pluralized, so 'User' uses "users"

Example: User.findOne({ email }) is a model method and returns a document. user.name = 'Ali'; await user.save() is a document method that saves only the changed fields.

Common mistake: Calling mongoose.model('User', schema) twice, for example in a hot-reload setup. It throws OverwriteModelError. Use mongoose.models.User || mongoose.model('User', schema).

Interview tip: Mention schema.methods for document helpers (user.comparePassword()) and schema.statics for model helpers (User.findByEmail()).

questions.question: How does validation work in Mongoose, and does it run on updates?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Validators run automatically on save() and create(). On update methods like updateOne and findOneAndUpdate they do not run unless you pass { runValidators: true }.

How it works:
Built-in: required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, enum, match
Custom: validate: { validator: (v) => ..., message: '...' }
Errors: a ValidationError with an errors object per field
Update validators: run only on the fields in the update, and "this" is not the document

Example: Schema says score: { type: Number, min: 0, max: 10 }. Quiz.create({ score: 15 }) fails. Quiz.updateOne({ _id }, { score: 15 }) saves 15, unless runValidators: true is set.

Common mistake: Relying on validation in an edit route that uses findByIdAndUpdate. Bad data gets in through updates even though create is protected.

Interview tip: Mention you can turn it on for every query with mongoose.set('runValidators', true), and that "unique" is not a validator. It only creates an index, and duplicates fail with error code 11000.
questions.codeSnippet:
await Quiz.findByIdAndUpdate(id, { score: 15 }, { runValidators: true, new: true });
// throws ValidationError: score must be <= 10

questions.question: What does populate() do in Mongoose, and how is it different from $lookup?
questions.answer:
Short answer: populate() replaces an ObjectId reference with the actual document from another collection. It does this with a second query from Node, while $lookup joins inside the database in one aggregation.

How it works:
ref: the field has { type: ObjectId, ref: 'User' }
populate('author', 'name avatar'): loads only the fields you need
Queries: one query for the posts, one find({ _id: { $in: ids } }) for all authors
Nested: populate({ path: 'comments', populate: { path: 'user' } })

Example: Post.find().populate('author', 'name').limit(20) runs 2 queries in total, not 21, and returns posts with author: { _id, name }.

Common mistake: Populating deep chains (post, then comments, then users, then their profiles). Each level is another query and loads lots of data, so pages slow down.

Interview tip: Say you use populate for simple reference loading in normal app code, and $lookup when you also need to filter, group or sort by fields of the joined data in the database.

questions.question: What are Mongoose middleware (hooks), and what is the difference between document and query middleware?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Middleware are functions that run before (pre) or after (post) certain operations. Document middleware runs on save() and validate(), with "this" as the document. Query middleware runs on find, updateOne and similar, with "this" as the query.

How it works:
Document hooks: save, validate, deleteOne (with document option)
Query hooks: find, findOne, updateOne, findOneAndUpdate, deleteMany
Aggregate hooks: aggregate
isModified: inside pre('save'), check if a field changed before doing work

Example: pre('save') hashes the password only when this.isModified('password'), so editing the user's name does not hash the already hashed password again.

Common mistake: Expecting pre('save') to run on findByIdAndUpdate. It does not, so a password changed through an update route is stored in plain text.

Interview tip: Mention a common query hook: pre(/^find/) that adds { isDeleted: false } to every find, so soft-deleted records are hidden everywhere.

questions.question: What does lean() do in a Mongoose query, and when should you use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: lean() returns plain JavaScript objects instead of full Mongoose documents. It is faster and uses less memory, but you lose document features like save(), getters, virtuals and change tracking.

How it works:
Without lean: each result is a document with methods and internal state
With lean: plain objects straight from the driver
Typical gain: lower memory and faster queries for large read-only lists

Example: The public question list API only reads and sends JSON. Question.find(filter).lean() is the right choice. The admin edit page that loads a question, changes it and calls save() should not use lean.

Common mistake: Using lean() and then calling doc.save() or expecting a virtual like fullName to be there. save is not a function on a plain object, and virtuals are missing unless you add a plugin such as mongoose-lean-virtuals.

Interview tip: Say your rule: "lean for reading and sending, full documents for changing and saving".

questions.question: What are virtuals in Mongoose, and why might they not show up in your API response?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Virtuals are computed properties that are not stored in MongoDB, like fullName from firstName and lastName. They are not included in toJSON() or toObject() by default, so res.json(user) leaves them out.

How it works:
Getter: schema.virtual('fullName').get(function () { ... })
Show in JSON: new Schema({...}, { toJSON: { virtuals: true } })
Not queryable: you cannot filter or sort by a virtual in MongoDB
Virtual populate: a virtual that loads related documents by a foreign field, like a user's posts

Example: A user schema has a virtual "isPro" based on plan and planExpiresAt. The React profile page shows undefined until you set toJSON: { virtuals: true }.

Common mistake: Using lean() on the query. Lean results are plain objects, so virtuals are not added at all, even with the toJSON option.

Interview tip: Mention virtual populate as a neat way to show "posts by this user" without storing an array of post ids on the user, avoiding a growing array.

questions.question: A profile update route runs User.findByIdAndUpdate(req.user.id, req.body). What problems does this have, and how do you fix them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It trusts the whole body (mass assignment), skips validators, skips save hooks, and returns the old document. Pick allowed fields, turn on validators and ask for the new document.

How it works: The problems:
Mass assignment: a user sends { "role": "admin" } or { "accessScope": "all" } and gets them
No validation: update validators are off by default
No pre('save'): a password in the body is stored without hashing
Old data: the method returns the document before the update unless new: true

Example: An attacker adds "role": "admin" to the edit-profile request in the browser dev tools and becomes an admin.

Common mistake: Removing role in the frontend form only. The API must decide which fields are allowed, because anyone can send any JSON.

Interview tip: Show a whitelist with only name and avatar, use { new: true, runValidators: true }, and handle password changes in a separate route that loads the document and calls save().

questions.question: How should you manage the Mongoose connection in an Express app, and what changes on serverless platforms?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Connect once when the app starts, reuse that connection (it has a pool) for every request, and start listening only after it connects. On serverless, cache the connection between invocations instead of connecting on every call.

How it works:
Connect once: await mongoose.connect(uri) in server.js, not inside routes
Pool: maxPoolSize (100 by default in the driver) controls parallel operations
Events: listen to 'error' and 'disconnected' and log them
Shutdown: on SIGTERM close the HTTP server, then mongoose.connection.close()
Serverless: keep the connection promise in a global variable so warm invocations reuse it

Example: On Vercel functions, connecting on every request quickly hits Atlas connection limits (500 on the free tier). Caching the promise keeps it to one connection per warm instance.

Common mistake: Calling mongoose.connect() inside each route handler. It creates new connections and slows every request.

Interview tip: Mention bufferCommands: Mongoose queues queries until connected, which can hide a failed connection as slow requests, so fail fast on startup errors.

questions.question: What do the strict and strictQuery options do in Mongoose, and how can a typo in a filter field cause a dangerous bug?
questions.answer:
Short answer: strict (on by default) silently drops fields that are not in the schema when saving. strictQuery controls the same for query filters. If unknown filter fields are removed, a typo can turn a filter into {} and match every document.

How it works:
strict true: unknown fields in new or updated data are ignored
strict 'throw': unknown fields cause an error
strictQuery false: unknown filter fields are kept (the default since Mongoose 7)
strictQuery true: unknown filter fields are removed from the filter

Example: With strictQuery: true, User.deleteMany({ emial: 'x@y.com' }) has its unknown "emial" removed, the filter becomes {}, and every user is deleted. With the default false, the filter stays and matches nothing.

Common mistake: Turning strictQuery on "for safety" without knowing this effect, or relying on strict to report typos in saved data, when it drops them without any error.

Interview tip: Mention strict: 'throw' during development so typos fail loudly, and always check deletedCount on destructive operations.
questions.codeSnippet:
mongoose.set('strictQuery', false); // default in Mongoose 7+

const schema = new mongoose.Schema({ name: String }, { strict: 'throw' });

questions.question: Which call creates a Mongoose model from a schema?
options: new mongoose.Schema("User", userSchema)
mongoose.model("User", userSchema)
mongoose.create("User", userSchema)
userSchema.model("User")
questions.correctAnswer: mongoose.model("User", userSchema)
questions.answer:
Why B: mongoose.model(name, schema) compiles the schema into a model linked to the "users" collection.

Why not A: new Schema() defines the shape. It does not take a model name.

Why not C: mongoose.create does not exist. Model.create() inserts documents.

Why not D: Schemas do not have a model() method.

questions.question: What happens when you call await User.findById("abc") with an invalid id string?
options: It returns null
It returns every user
It rejects with a CastError ("Cast to ObjectId failed")
It creates a new ObjectId and returns null
questions.correctAnswer: It rejects with a CastError ("Cast to ObjectId failed")
questions.answer:
Why C: Mongoose tries to cast "abc" to an ObjectId, fails, and rejects the query with a CastError.

Why not A: null is returned for a valid id that does not exist, not for an invalid one.

Why not B: The filter is not dropped, so it never returns all users.

Why not D: Mongoose does not replace bad input with a new id.

Fix: Check mongoose.isValidObjectId(id) and return 400, or handle CastError in the error middleware.

questions.question: The schema has age: { type: Number, min: 18 }. What happens with User.updateOne({ _id: id }, { age: 10 })?
options: The update is rejected with a ValidationError
Age is saved as 18, the minimum
The age change is ignored and nothing is saved
Age is saved as 10, because update validators are off by default
questions.correctAnswer: Age is saved as 10, because update validators are off by default
questions.answer:
Why D: Validators run on save() and create(), but update queries skip them unless runValidators: true is passed.

Why not A: That only happens with { runValidators: true } or mongoose.set('runValidators', true).

Why not B: Mongoose never clamps values to the minimum.

Why not C: The update is a normal $set of age, so it is applied.

questions.question: What do you get from await User.find().lean()?
options: Plain JavaScript objects, without Mongoose methods or virtuals
Mongoose documents with save() and virtuals
A cursor that you must call toArray() on
A JSON string
questions.correctAnswer: Plain JavaScript objects, without Mongoose methods or virtuals
questions.answer:
Why A: lean() skips building Mongoose documents and returns plain objects from the driver.

Why not B: That is the result without lean().

Why not C: Mongoose returns an array for awaited find queries. A cursor needs .cursor().

Why not D: The results are objects. Express turns them into JSON later with res.json().

questions.question: A pre("save") hook hashes the password. A route then runs User.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: id }, { password: "new123" }). What happens?
options: The hook runs and the password is hashed
Mongoose throws, because password changes need save()
The hook does not run, so "new123" is stored in plain text
The hook runs only if runValidators is true
questions.correctAnswer: The hook does not run, so "new123" is stored in plain text
questions.answer:
Why C: findOneAndUpdate triggers query middleware, not document save middleware, so the hashing code never runs.

Why not A: pre("save") is only for save() and create().

Why not B: Mongoose allows updating any field. It does not know your field is special.

Why not D: runValidators turns on update validators, not save hooks.

Fix: Load the user, set user.password, call save(), or hash it in a pre("findOneAndUpdate") hook.

questions.question: The schema has only a name field, with default options. What happens with await new User({ name: "Ali", nickname: "Alu" }).save()?
options: The document is saved with both name and nickname
save() throws a strict mode error
The document is saved with nickname: null
The document is saved with name only, and nickname is dropped silently
questions.correctAnswer: The document is saved with name only, and nickname is dropped silently
questions.answer:
Why D: strict is true by default, so fields not in the schema are removed without any error.

Why not A: Unknown fields are only kept with strict: false.

Why not B: An error only happens with strict: "throw".

Why not C: The field is not set to null. It is simply not saved.
